**2.6** For the avoidance of doubt, where any term is defined in both this Paragraph 2 and in Annex II, the Annex II definition shall govern.

**3.4** A Confirmation shall, upon delivery, supplement, form part of, and be subject to this Agreement. Together with this Agreement, each Confirmation shall evidence a complete and binding agreement between the parties with respect to the Transaction to which it relates. In the event of any inconsistency between the terms of a Confirmation and the terms of this Agreement (including Annex I and Annex II), the terms of the Confirmation shall prevail with respect to the Transaction to which such Confirmation relates, unless the Confirmation expressly provides otherwise.

**4.4** Upon the existence of a Margin Deficit, Buyer may by notice to Seller (a \"**Margin Call**\") require Seller to transfer to Buyer Additional Purchased Securities or Cash Margin (or any combination thereof) in an amount sufficient to eliminate such Margin Deficit (the aggregate amount so required, the \"**Delivery Amount**\"). Notwithstanding the foregoing, no transfer shall be required if the Delivery Amount would be less than or equal to the applicable Margin Threshold specified in Annex II, Section 5(a) (being \$250,000 as of the date hereof).

**4.5** Upon the existence of a Margin Excess, Seller may by notice to Buyer (also a \"**Margin Call**\") require Buyer to transfer to Seller Equivalent Securities or Cash Margin (or any combination thereof) sufficient to eliminate such Margin Excess (the aggregate amount so required, the \"**Return Amount**\"). Notwithstanding the foregoing, no transfer shall be required if the Return Amount would be less than or equal to the applicable Margin Threshold specified in Annex II, Section 5(b) (being \$250,000 as of the date hereof).

**4.6** Any Additional Purchased Securities transferred by Seller to Buyer pursuant to a Margin Call must constitute Eligible Collateral, and the Market Value of such Additional Purchased Securities (after application of the relevant Haircut Percentage) shall be at least equal to the Delivery Amount.

**4.7** A Margin Call must be received by the other party by the margin call cut-off time specified in Annex II, Section 7 (being 10:00 a.m. London time as of the date hereof) in order for the resulting transfer to be required on that same Business Day.

**4.10** For the purposes of this Paragraph 4(c), a Margin Call shall be deemed to have been \"received\" when it is actually received by the recipient at the address, facsimile number, or electronic mail address specified in Annex II, Section 14 for the giving of notices. Each party shall use commercially reasonable efforts to acknowledge receipt of a Margin Call promptly upon receipt.
**4.11** The applicable Haircut Percentage for each category of Eligible Collateral is as specified in Annex II, Section 4, and is summarised as follows:
Eligible Sovereign Securities       2.0% (the \"Sovereign Haircut\")
Eligible Corporate Securities       5.0% (the \"Corporate Haircut\")

**4.12** The Transaction Exposure in respect of any Transaction shall be calculated by applying the relevant Haircut Percentage to the Market Value of the Purchased Securities. The Haircut Percentage shall be applied in the manner set out in Annex II, Section 4, such that the Purchase Price for a Transaction shall be determined by dividing the Market Value of the Purchased Securities by one (1) plus the applicable Haircut Percentage (expressed as a decimal).

**4.13** Buyer reserves the right, upon not less than five (5) Business Days\' prior written notice to Seller, to revise the applicable Haircut Percentage for any category of Eligible Collateral in connection with future Transactions, provided that (a) any such revision shall apply only to Transactions entered into after the effective date of such revision and shall not affect the terms of any Transaction already outstanding, and (b) any such revision shall be made in good faith and on a commercially reasonable basis, having regard to prevailing market conditions, the credit quality of the relevant class of securities, and Buyer\'s internal risk management policies.

**5.1** Where Purchased Securities are held by Buyer on a record date, ex-dividend date, or other relevant date for any distribution of Income (including, without limitation, any coupon, interest payment, dividend, principal repayment (other than at maturity), or other distribution payable in respect of such Purchased Securities), Buyer shall, on the next Business Day following the date on which Buyer receives or is credited with such Income, pay to Seller an amount equal to such Income (a \"**Manufactured Payment**\").

**5.2** Manufactured Payments shall be made in the currency in which the relevant Income payment is denominated and shall be paid to the account designated by Seller for the receipt of funds in such currency, as specified in the relevant Confirmation or as otherwise notified by Seller to Buyer in writing.

**5.3** All Manufactured Payments shall be made net of any applicable withholding tax, deduction, or other amount required to be withheld or deducted by Buyer under applicable law. If Buyer is required by applicable law to make any such withholding or deduction, the provisions of Paragraph 11 (Tax) shall apply with respect to any obligation of Buyer to gross up such payment.

**5.4** For the avoidance of doubt, the obligation to make a Manufactured Payment arises regardless of whether Buyer has actually received the relevant Income payment from the issuer of the Purchased Securities. Buyer\'s obligation to make the Manufactured Payment is an independent obligation under this Agreement and shall not be conditional upon Buyer\'s receipt of the underlying Income.

**6.1** All payments of cash required to be made under this Agreement shall be made in immediately available, freely transferable, same-day funds in the relevant currency to the account specified by the receiving party in the relevant Confirmation, in Annex II, Section 14, or as otherwise notified by the receiving party to the paying party in writing from time to time.

> Application: The Purchase Price for a Transaction in which the Purchased Securities are Eligible Sovereign Securities shall be determined by dividing the Market Value of such Purchased Securities (as of the relevant Purchase Date or, in the case of Additional Purchased Securities, as of the date of transfer) by 1.020.
> *Illustrative example:* If the Market Value of Eligible Sovereign Securities is \$100,000,000, the Purchase Price shall be \$100,000,000 ÷ 1.020 = \$98,039,215.69.
**(b) Eligible Corporate Securities:**
> Haircut Percentage: **5.0%** (the \"**Corporate Haircut**\").

> Application: The Purchase Price for a Transaction in which the Purchased Securities are Eligible Corporate Securities shall be determined by dividing the Market Value of such Purchased Securities (as of the relevant Purchase Date or, in the case of Additional Purchased Securities, as of the date of transfer) by 1.050.
> *Illustrative example:* If the Market Value of Eligible Corporate Securities is \$50,000,000, the Purchase Price shall be \$50,000,000 ÷ 1.050 = \$47,619,047.62.

**(c)** The Haircut Percentages set out in this Section 4 shall apply to the initial pricing of each Transaction and to the valuation of Purchased Securities and Additional Purchased Securities for the purposes of Paragraph 4 (Margin Maintenance). For the avoidance of doubt, the Haircut Percentage applicable to a Transaction shall be determined by reference to the category of Eligible Collateral into which the relevant Purchased Securities fall at the time of the initial Transaction and shall not change during the life of that Transaction unless the Purchased Securities are substituted in accordance with Paragraph 8 and Annex II, Section 9, in which case the Haircut Percentage applicable to the Alternative Securities shall apply from the date of substitution.
**Section 5 --- Margin Thresholds**
**(a) Delivery Amount (Margin Deficit --- payable by Seller):**
> Margin Threshold: **\$250,000** (two hundred fifty thousand United States Dollars).

> No obligation to deliver Additional Purchased Securities or Cash Margin arises unless the Delivery Amount (calculated in the Base Currency on an aggregate net basis across all outstanding Transactions) exceeds \$250,000.
**(b) Return Amount (Margin Excess --- payable by Buyer):**
> Margin Threshold: **\$250,000** (two hundred fifty thousand United States Dollars).

> No obligation to return Equivalent Securities or Cash Margin arises unless the Return Amount (calculated in the Base Currency on an aggregate net basis across all outstanding Transactions) exceeds \$250,000.

**(c)** The Margin Thresholds set forth in sub-paragraphs (a) and (b) above apply on an aggregate net basis across all outstanding Transactions. For the avoidance of doubt, the Margin Threshold is not applied on a per-Transaction basis; rather, the aggregate Delivery Amount or Return Amount across all Transactions must exceed the applicable Margin Threshold before any transfer obligation arises.
**Section 6 --- Net Exposure Cap**

**6.1** The aggregate net exposure of Buyer to Seller under all Transactions outstanding at any time shall not exceed **\$1,500,000,000** (one billion five hundred million United States Dollars) (the \"**Net Exposure Cap**\").

**6.2** For the purposes of this Section 6, \"**net exposure**\" means the aggregate Transaction Exposure of all outstanding Transactions (after application of the relevant Haircuts and after deduction of any Cash Margin held by or on behalf of Buyer), calculated in the Base Currency as of the most recent mark-to-market determination.

**6.3** If at any time the net exposure would exceed the Net Exposure Cap (whether as a result of a proposed new Transaction, a decline in the Market Value of Purchased Securities, or otherwise), Buyer shall not be required to enter into any further Transaction and Seller shall, promptly upon notice from Buyer, deliver additional Eligible Collateral or cash in an amount sufficient to reduce the net exposure below the Net Exposure Cap. Failure by Seller to make such delivery within one (1) Business Day of receipt of such notice shall constitute a failure to comply with a Margin Call for the purposes of Paragraph 10(a)(ii).
**6.4** The Net Exposure Cap may be amended from time to time by mutual written agreement of the parties.
**Section 7 --- Margin Call Cut-off Time and Settlement**
**(a)** The margin call cut-off time shall be **10:00 a.m. London time** on a Business Day.

**(b)** If a Margin Call is given and received before 10:00 a.m. London time on a Business Day, the resulting transfer of Additional Purchased Securities, Equivalent Securities, or Cash Margin (as applicable) shall be effected on that **same Business Day**.

**(c)** If a Margin Call is given or received at or after 10:00 a.m. London time on a Business Day, or on a day that is not a Business Day, the resulting transfer shall be effected on the **next following Business Day**.

**(d)** For the purposes of this Section 7, a Margin Call shall be deemed to have been \"received\" at the time of actual receipt by the addressee at the notice details specified in Section 14 of this Annex II. Each party shall use commercially reasonable efforts to respond to and acknowledge receipt of a Margin Call promptly upon receipt.
**Section 8 --- Netting**

Paragraph 7(b) of the Agreement (settlement netting for obligations in the same currency falling due on the same settlement date) is **elected and applicable**. Accordingly, where on any Business Day amounts would otherwise be payable in the same currency and on the same settlement date by each party to the other under this Agreement, such amounts shall be netted in accordance with Paragraph 7(b) of the Agreement, and only the resulting net amount shall be payable by the party owing such amount.
**Section 9 --- Substitution**

**(a)** Seller may, from time to time during the term of any Transaction, request the substitution of Alternative Securities for all or any part of the Purchased Securities in that Transaction. Any such request shall be made in writing (including by electronic mail) and shall specify in reasonable detail the Purchased Securities to be replaced, the proposed Alternative Securities (including ISIN, nominal amount, issuer, coupon, maturity, and credit rating), and the proposed substitution date.

**(b)** Any such substitution shall require the **prior written consent of Buyer**. Buyer may grant, withhold, condition, or delay such consent in its sole and absolute discretion and shall not be required to provide any reason for any refusal. Buyer shall use reasonable efforts to respond to any request for substitution within two (2) Business Days of receipt, but any failure to respond within such period shall not constitute consent.

**(c)** Where Buyer consents, the substitution shall be effected on the Business Day agreed by the parties (or, failing agreement, on the second Business Day following Buyer\'s consent) by simultaneous transfer of the Alternative Securities to Buyer (or to Buyer\'s account at the relevant settlement system) and the Purchased Securities to Seller (or to Seller\'s account at the relevant settlement system), through the applicable settlement system in accordance with Paragraph 6.

**(d)** Alternative Securities must qualify as Eligible Collateral and must satisfy all of the eligibility criteria set out in Section 3 of this Annex II. The Market Value of the Alternative Securities (after application of the relevant Haircut Percentage) must be at least equal to the Market Value of the Purchased Securities being replaced (after application of the relevant Haircut Percentage) as of the close of business on the Business Day immediately preceding the substitution date. If the Alternative Securities fall into a different category of Eligible Collateral than the Purchased Securities being replaced, the Haircut Percentage applicable to the Alternative Securities shall apply from the date of substitution.

**(e)** Upon completion of a substitution, the Alternative Securities shall become the Purchased Securities for all purposes of the relevant Transaction, and the Confirmation for such Transaction shall be deemed to have been amended accordingly. For the avoidance of doubt, the occurrence of a substitution shall not affect the Purchase Date, the Repurchase Date, or the Pricing Rate of the relevant Transaction, unless otherwise agreed by the parties.
**Section 10 --- Cross-Default**
**(a)** For the purposes of Paragraph 10(a)(vi) of the Agreement, a \"**Cross-Default**\" shall occur with respect to a party if:

> \(i\) such party fails to make any payment or delivery when due (after giving effect to any applicable grace period) under one or more agreements or instruments relating to Specified Indebtedness in an aggregate amount exceeding the Cross-Default Threshold; or

> \(ii\) such party\'s Specified Indebtedness in an aggregate amount exceeding the Cross-Default Threshold is accelerated, or becomes capable of being accelerated, prior to its stated maturity as a result of a default (howsoever described) thereunder; or

> \(iii\) any security interest securing Specified Indebtedness in an aggregate amount exceeding the Cross-Default Threshold becomes enforceable and is enforced (including by the taking of possession or the appointment of a receiver, administrative receiver, manager, or other similar officer).

**(b)** \"**Specified Indebtedness**\" means any obligation (whether present or future, contingent or otherwise, as principal or surety or otherwise) in respect of borrowed money. For the avoidance of doubt, Specified Indebtedness includes obligations under loan agreements, credit facilities, overdraft facilities, note purchase agreements, bond indentures, guarantees of borrowed money, and similar instruments, but excludes obligations under this Agreement and under any other agreement that is a GMRA, GMSLA, or ISDA Master Agreement between the parties.

**(c)** \"**Cross-Default Threshold**\" means, with respect to each party, **\$10,000,000** (ten million United States Dollars) (or its equivalent in any other currency, converted into the Base Currency at the spot rate of exchange at the relevant time).

**(d)** For the purposes of determining whether the Cross-Default Threshold has been exceeded, all amounts of Specified Indebtedness in respect of which the relevant event has occurred shall be aggregated (regardless of whether such amounts arise under the same or different agreements or instruments).
**Section 11 --- Act of Insolvency**
**(a)** The definition of \"Act of Insolvency\" shall be as set out in the 2011 ICMA GMRA, supplemented as follows.

**(b)** **Grace Period: None (zero days).** An Act of Insolvency shall constitute an Event of Default immediately and automatically upon occurrence, without requirement for notice or lapse of any period of time (an \"**ipso facto trigger**\"). For the avoidance of doubt, upon the occurrence of an Act of Insolvency with respect to a party, the other party shall be entitled, without the requirement for any notice to the Defaulting Party, to designate an Early Termination Date in respect of all outstanding Transactions in accordance with Paragraph 10(b).

**(c)** For the avoidance of doubt, and without limiting the definition of Act of Insolvency set out in the 2011 ICMA GMRA, each of the following shall constitute an Act of Insolvency for the purposes of this Agreement:

> \(i\) the appointment of a receiver, administrator, liquidator, conservator, trustee, custodian, or similar official over a party or any material part of its assets, whether by a court of competent jurisdiction, a governmental or regulatory authority, or otherwise;

> \(ii\) the filing of any petition, application, or proceeding (whether voluntary or involuntary) seeking any such appointment or seeking any arrangement, reorganisation, composition, readjustment, liquidation, dissolution, winding-up, or similar relief under any applicable insolvency, bankruptcy, receivership, administration, or similar law;
> \(iii\) the making of a general assignment for the benefit of creditors;
> \(iv\) the admission in writing by a party of its inability to pay its debts generally as they become due;
> \(v\) the taking of any corporate or other action by a party in furtherance of any of the foregoing; or
> \(vi\) any analogous event or proceeding in any jurisdiction.
**Section 12 --- Repricing / Mini Close-out**

**(a)** Buyer may, at its sole option, elect to reprice any Transaction having an original term or, in the case of an evergreen or rolling Transaction, a then-current term, exceeding sixty (60) calendar days. Such repricing (a \"**Repricing Event**\") may be exercised on the **90th calendar day** following the Purchase Date of the relevant Transaction, or on the anniversary of any prior Repricing Date if the Transaction remains outstanding (each such date, a \"**Repricing Date**\"). If a Repricing Date falls on a day that is not a Business Day, the Repricing Date shall be the next following Business Day.

**(b)** Buyer shall exercise a Repricing Event by delivering written notice to Seller not less than two (2) Business Days prior to the applicable Repricing Date. Such notice shall specify the Transaction to be repriced and the proposed Repricing Date.
**(c)** Upon the occurrence of a Repricing Event:

> \(i\) the original Transaction shall terminate on the Repricing Date as if such date were the Repurchase Date, and Seller shall pay to Buyer the Repurchase Price applicable to the original Transaction as of the Repricing Date;
> \(ii\) simultaneously, the parties shall enter into a new Transaction on terms identical to the original Transaction, save that:
> \(A\) the Purchase Date of the new Transaction shall be the Repricing Date;

> \(B\) the Purchase Price of the new Transaction shall be recalculated based on the Market Value of the Purchased Securities on the Repricing Date (after application of the relevant Haircut Percentage); and

> \(C\) the Pricing Rate shall be as agreed by the parties or, failing agreement by 5:00 p.m. London time on the Business Day immediately preceding the Repricing Date, the Pricing Rate applicable to the original Transaction shall continue to apply to the new Transaction;

> \(iii\) the close-out amount, if any, arising from the termination of the original Transaction and the simultaneous commencement of the new Transaction shall be calculated as the difference between the Repurchase Price of the original Transaction and the Purchase Price of the new Transaction. Such close-out amount shall be settled in cash on the Repricing Date by the party owing the net amount to the other party.

**(d)** The repricing mechanic set out in this Section 12 does not affect either party\'s rights under Paragraph 4 (Margin Maintenance) or Paragraph 10 (Events of Default). For the avoidance of doubt, the existence of a Repricing Event or the exercise of a Repricing Event shall not relieve either party of its obligations to make margin transfers or to comply with Margin Calls during the period between the date of notice and the Repricing Date.

**(e)** The parties acknowledge that the purpose of the repricing mechanic is to adjust the economic terms of outstanding Transactions to reflect current market conditions and to manage the credit exposure of the parties. The new Transaction entered into on a Repricing Date shall, for all purposes of this Agreement, be treated as a new and separate Transaction.
**Section 13 --- Tax Gross-Up**
**(a)** Paragraph 11(b) of the Agreement (Tax Gross-Up) is **elected and applicable**.

**(b)** If a Tax Payor fails to pay any additional amounts required under Paragraph 11(b), the Tax Payee shall give written notice of such failure to the Tax Payor. The Tax Payor shall have a cure period of **five (5) Business Days** from receipt of such written notice within which to pay the outstanding Tax Gross-Up Amount in full.

**(c)** Failure of the Tax Payor to cure such failure within such five (5) Business Day period shall constitute an **Event of Default** with respect to the Tax Payor, and the Tax Payee may thereafter exercise its rights under Paragraph 10(b) of the Agreement, including the right to designate an Early Termination Date in respect of all outstanding Transactions.
**Section 14 --- Notices**
**(a) Buyer:**
> Address: Voss Bank AG, London Branch, 25 Ropemaker Street, 12th Floor, London EC2Y 9LY, United Kingdom
> Attention: Henrik J. Lindqvist, Director --- Collateral Trading & Legal

**(b) Seller:**

> Attention: Dana R. Castellano, Managing Director --- Treasury & Secured Funding

> Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP 570 Lexington Avenue, 30th Floor, New York, NY 10022, USA
> Attention: Rachel S. Okonkwo
> Email: rokonkwo@pryorag.com
**Section 15 --- Settlement Systems**
**(a)** For Euro-denominated Eligible Collateral: **Clearstream Banking S.A.** (42 Avenue JF Kennedy, L-1855 Luxembourg).
**(b)** For USD-denominated Eligible Collateral: **The Depository Trust Company (DTC)** (55 Water Street, New York, NY 10041, USA).

**(c)** Tri-party custodial arrangements are **not applicable** as of the date hereof. The parties note that BNY Meliora Trust Company, N.A. has been identified as the potential tri-party custodian if the parties subsequently elect to include a tri-party annexe. Any future election of tri-party custodial arrangements shall require a written amendment to this Agreement signed by both parties and shall be documented in a separate tri-party custodial agreement or annexe.
**Section 16 --- Income Payments**

Manufactured Payments due from Buyer to Seller pursuant to Paragraph 5 of this Agreement shall be made on the **next Business Day following the relevant record date** for the distribution of Income on the Purchased Securities. For the avoidance of doubt, the obligation to make a Manufactured Payment arises on the Business Day following the record date, regardless of the actual payment date of the underlying Income distribution by the issuer of the Purchased Securities.
**Section 17 --- Buy/Sell Back Transactions**

**Not Applicable.** The parties do not intend to enter into Buy/Sell Back Transactions under this Agreement. If the parties wish to enter into Buy/Sell Back Transactions, they shall negotiate and agree a separate annex or amendment to this Agreement addressing such Transactions.

block.text:
**Planning Arbitration Clause Updates**

I’m thinking about replacing the tracking part with LCIA clause and expedited procedure for amounts under 5 million. It seems I should include that English law remains unchanged and accepted. I'd then replace section 17.3 with full LCIA arbitration, 17.4 with the seat details, 17.5 with the expedited procedure mechanism, and consider retaining interim relief in section 17.6. It all feels quite straightforward but I’ll double-check my wording for clarity.

**Creating workbook structure**

I’m laying out a new workbook with various sheets. The first one will be the "Issues Tracker," featuring columns like Issue #, Category, Issue Description, GMRA Cross-Reference, and several others about negotiation dynamics and positions. Rows 1-3 will have resolved issues with final terms, while row 4 will be open for repricing. This setup aims to keep everything organized and clear as we move forward. Sounds like a solid plan!

**Organizing draft mark-ups**

I’m drafting mark-ups with a status of “Open” and advancing. Line 19: This document sets forth the standard negotiation positions, acceptable ranges, and walk-away parameters for Meridian Capital Securities LLC (\"Meridian,\" \"the Firm,\" CRD# 298417, EIN 83-2947561, LEI 5493007XKBT49LP2QR12) in the negotiation of Global Master Repurchase Agreements (\"GMRAs\") and Master Repurchase Agreements (\"MRAs\") with bank counterparties. All personnel on the Treasury & Secured Funding desk --- including traders, desk analysts, desk heads, and any other front-office personnel involved in onboarding or re-papering counterparty relationships --- and outside counsel (currently Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP, as further described in Section 13) must adhere to the positions and escalation procedures described herein. Failure to comply with these guidelines may result in disciplinary action, including but not limited to removal of negotiation authority and referral to the Firm\'s Compliance Department.
Line 25: > \(b\) All material amendments to existing GMRAs and MRAs, including amendments that modify haircut levels, margin provisions, events of default, cross-default thresholds, substitution rights, repricing triggers, governing law, or dispute resolution mechanisms;
Line 37: > • Meridian acts as Seller in substantially all repo transactions contemplated by these guidelines. The positions and ranges set forth herein are calibrated to Meridian\'s role as Seller. In the rare circumstance that Meridian acts as Buyer, the desk must consult with the General Counsel before applying these guidelines, as certain provisions (including haircut targets and substitution rights) may require adjustment.
Line 45: > • These guidelines are informed by Meridian\'s audited net capital of \$412,000,000 as of 31 December 2024, as determined in accordance with SEC Rule 15c3-1 (the \"Net Capital Rule\") under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended. All thresholds expressed as percentages of net capital are calculated on that basis and must be re-evaluated upon each quarterly net capital recertification. The Office of the CFO circulates quarterly net capital certifications to the desk, the General Counsel, and Risk Management within five business days following the end of each fiscal quarter. If a quarterly recertification reveals a change in net capital that would alter the dollar amounts implied by percentage thresholds set forth herein (e.g., the cross-default walk-away analysis in Section 7.1), the desk must coordinate with the General Counsel to determine whether an interim revision of these guidelines is warranted.
Line 53: **2.1 --- Overriding Objective.** Meridian\'s overriding objective in repo documentation negotiations is to maintain operational flexibility in collateral management while preserving robust netting and close-out protections. Operational flexibility --- particularly the ability to substitute collateral without undue delay or counterparty consent, to manage margin calls within reasonable timeframes, and to avoid unnecessary repricing events during the life of a transaction --- is essential to the efficient functioning of Meridian\'s secured funding business. At the same time, the integrity of netting and close-out provisions is critical to Meridian\'s regulatory capital treatment and insolvency protections. Negotiators must balance these two objectives and should not sacrifice one in pursuit of the other.
Line 59: > • **Acceptable positions** represent the range within which the desk and outside counsel may agree to a counterparty\'s proposal without further escalation. Any position within the acceptable range is pre-approved for closing. The desk should exercise judgment in determining where within the acceptable range to settle; the midpoint of the range is generally a reasonable compromise and should be the desk\'s default counter-offer when a counterparty\'s opening position falls outside the acceptable range.
Line 61: > • **Walk-away positions** represent hard limits. Acceptance of terms beyond walk-away thresholds is prohibited without Managing Director and General Counsel joint approval, which will be granted only in exceptional circumstances and only after a written assessment of the commercial rationale and risk impact has been prepared and presented to both approvers. Walk-away overrides are expected to be rare; if the desk finds itself seeking walk-away overrides on a recurring basis with a particular counterparty or class of counterparties, the guidelines themselves may need to be revised, and the desk should raise this with the General Counsel.
Line 69: **2.6 --- Regulatory Awareness.** All negotiation positions and settlement outcomes must be consistent with Meridian\'s obligations under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Certain terms --- particularly haircut levels, cross-default thresholds, and margin provisions --- have a direct impact on Meridian\'s regulatory net capital computation. Negotiators are not expected to perform net capital calculations themselves but must be aware of the interaction between documentation terms and net capital requirements and must escalate any term that could have a material capital impact to the Office of the CFO through the procedures set forth in Section 9.
Line 71: **[Section 3 --- Haircuts (Pricing Rate / Purchase Price Discount)]{.underline}**
Line 73: Haircut levels --- referred to in certain GMRA contexts as the \"Pricing Rate\" or \"Purchase Price Discount\" and in certain MRA contexts as the \"Margin Percentage\" --- are among the most commercially significant terms in a repo agreement. The haircut determines the relationship between the Market Value of collateral delivered by the Seller and the Purchase Price received by the Seller. A higher haircut means the Seller receives less cash for a given amount of collateral, effectively increasing the Seller\'s cost of funding and reducing the efficiency of its collateral deployment.
Line 75: For purposes of these guidelines, \"haircut\" refers to the percentage by which the Purchase Price is discounted relative to the Market Value of the Purchased Securities. All illustrative calculations in this Section assume a simple one-minus-haircut formulation --- i.e., Purchase Price = Market Value × (1 − Haircut) --- unless otherwise indicated.
Line 79: Sovereign collateral is Meridian\'s primary collateral class for repo transactions and receives the most favorable haircut treatment from bank counterparties due to its high credit quality and deep secondary market liquidity.
Line 81: **Target:** Haircut of 1.5% or lower. At this level, \$100,000,000 in sovereign collateral at Market Value produces a Purchase Price of approximately \$98,522,167.49 (reflecting minor rounding adjustments for accrued interest and settlement date conventions that may apply in practice). The 1.5% target is consistent with haircut levels observed in bilateral repo transactions between U.S. broker-dealers and well-capitalized bank counterparties during the period from January 2024 through September 2024.
Line 83: **Acceptable:** Haircut up to 2.0%. The desk may agree to any figure at or below 2.0% without escalation. A midpoint settlement of 1.75% is a reasonable compromise and should be offered as a counter when the counterparty opens at 2.0% or above. At 1.75%, illustrative sovereign collateral with a Market Value of \$100,000,000 yields a Purchase Price of approximately \$98,280,098.28 (subject to the same rounding and convention adjustments noted above). The difference between the target of 1.5% and the acceptable ceiling of 2.0% represents a range of approximately \$500,000 in funding efficiency per \$100,000,000 of collateral deployed --- a meaningful but manageable cost within the desk\'s trading parameters.
Line 85: **Walk-away:** Haircuts above 2.0% for sovereign collateral are not acceptable. Any counterparty insistence on a sovereign haircut above 2.0% must be escalated per Section 9. In practice, a sovereign haircut above 2.0% from a well-capitalized bank counterparty is unusual and may indicate that the counterparty\'s credit or risk function has classified Meridian at an elevated risk tier, which should prompt a broader relationship discussion rather than a narrow documentation negotiation.
Line 87: **Eligible Sovereign Issuers:** The following sovereign issuers are eligible for the haircut levels specified above:
Line 103: All eligible sovereign issuers must be rated A-- (Standard & Poor\'s) / A3 (Moody\'s Investors Service) or above by at least one of the two foregoing rating agencies at the time of the relevant Transaction. If the sovereign credit rating of any G7 issuer falls below the minimum threshold during the life of a Transaction, the impact on existing positions must be assessed by Risk Management in consultation with the desk. The inclusion or exclusion of specific sovereign issuers in Annex I is a material negotiation point and should be confirmed with the desk before finalizing any agreement.
Line 107: Corporate collateral is Meridian\'s secondary collateral class for repo transactions. Due to the higher credit risk and lower secondary market liquidity of corporate debt securities relative to sovereign collateral, bank counterparties apply larger haircuts to corporate collateral.
Line 109: **Target:** Haircut of 3.5% or lower. At this level, \$50,000,000 in corporate collateral at Market Value produces a Purchase Price of approximately \$48,309,178.74. The 3.5% target is achievable with well-capitalized bank counterparties where the corporate collateral pool consists predominantly of investment-grade issues with short-to-medium residual maturities.
Line 111: **Acceptable:** Haircut up to 4.5%. The desk may agree to any figure at or below 4.5% without escalation. A midpoint settlement of 4.25% is a reasonable compromise and should be offered when the counterparty opens at 5.0% or above. At 4.25%, illustrative corporate collateral with a Market Value of \$50,000,000 yields a Purchase Price of approximately \$47,961,630.70. The desk should note that the spread between the target (3.5%) and the acceptable ceiling (4.5%) is wider for corporate collateral than for sovereign collateral, reflecting the greater variability in market practice for corporate haircuts and the desk\'s need for additional negotiation room.
Line 113: **Walk-away:** Haircuts above 4.5% for corporate collateral are not acceptable without escalation. Escalation must follow the procedures set forth in Section 9. Haircuts above 4.5% for investment-grade corporate collateral are indicative of an aggressive counterparty risk posture that warrants further review.
Line 127: **3.3 --- Haircut Negotiation Notes**
Line 131: > \(a\) When negotiating with well-capitalized European bank counterparties --- in particular, institutions with Common Equity Tier 1 (\"CET1\") capital in excess of CHF 5,000,000,000 or EUR equivalent --- counterparties frequently open at 2.0% for sovereign collateral and 5.0% for corporate collateral. These opening positions are well-established within European bank playbooks and should be treated as the starting point for negotiation rather than as final positions. The desk should counter at Meridian\'s target levels (1.5% sovereign / 3.5% corporate) and expect to settle at or near the respective midpoints (1.75% sovereign / 4.25% corporate).
Line 133: > \(b\) Certain counterparties may propose tiered haircut schedules that assign different haircut levels to different sovereign issuers (e.g., a lower haircut for U.S. Treasuries and a higher haircut for Italian government bonds). The desk may agree to reasonable tiered schedules provided that (i) all individual haircut levels fall within the ranges specified in Section 3.1 and (ii) the weighted average haircut across the projected collateral pool does not exceed the acceptable ceiling of 2.0%.
Line 135: > \(c\) Haircut levels directly affect Meridian\'s net capital charges under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Haircuts materially above the acceptable range increase the capital charge on repo positions because the excess haircut represents a deduction from net capital. Any haircut level that would result in incremental SEC Rule 15c3-1 net capital charges in excess of \$5,000,000 in aggregate across the projected transaction portfolio with the relevant counterparty must be flagged to the Office of the CFO before the desk or outside counsel conveys agreement to the counterparty. This escalation requirement applies regardless of whether the haircut level is within the acceptable range specified in this Section 3.
Line 137: > \(d\) The desk should avoid agreeing to haircut \"reopener\" or \"reset\" provisions that allow the counterparty to unilaterally increase haircuts during the life of a Transaction upon the occurrence of specified triggers (e.g., a rating downgrade of the Eligible Collateral issuer or a market volatility event). Such provisions transfer pricing risk to Meridian mid-transaction and are operationally disruptive. If a counterparty insists on a haircut reset mechanism, the desk should propose instead that any increased haircut apply only to new Transactions entered into after the trigger event, not to existing Transactions.
Line 141: Margin provisions govern the mechanics of collateral adjustments during the life of a Transaction and are central to both parties\' credit protection. The key margin provisions addressed in this Section are the Margin Threshold (the de minimis amount below which margin calls need not be made), margin call timing and settlement, and the Net Exposure Cap.
Line 143: **4.1 --- Margin Thresholds (Delivery Amounts)**
Line 145: The Margin Threshold (sometimes referred to as the \"Minimum Transfer Amount\" or \"Delivery Amount Threshold\") is the minimum Net Exposure that must exist before either party is obligated to deliver margin. Thresholds that are too low generate a high volume of small margin calls that impose disproportionate operational costs; thresholds that are too high leave excessive uncollateralized exposure.
Line 147: **Target:** \$500,000 symmetric --- that is, a Margin Threshold of \$500,000 applies equally to both Seller\'s and Buyer\'s obligation to deliver margin. The symmetric formulation is commercially balanced and straightforward to administer. At a \$500,000 threshold and an assumed average transaction size of \$250,000,000 to \$500,000,000, margin calls will be triggered only when Net Exposure exceeds a de minimis level, reducing operational friction without creating material credit exposure.
Line 149: **Acceptable:** Asymmetric thresholds, provided the Seller (Meridian) Margin Threshold is no lower than \$500,000. In practice, certain bank counterparties --- particularly those with large settlement operations and automated margin call systems --- seek lower thresholds to minimize their uncollateralized exposure to non-bank counterparties. The desk may agree to a Buyer Margin Threshold as low as \$250,000 where the counterparty insists on asymmetry --- that is, a \$500,000 threshold for Seller (Meridian) deliveries and a \$250,000 threshold for Buyer (counterparty) deliveries. This asymmetric formulation benefits the counterparty by requiring Meridian to deliver margin at a lower threshold when the counterparty is owed margin, while preserving Meridian\'s \$500,000 threshold when Meridian is owed margin. The desk should agree to this formulation only if the counterparty provides a reasonable commercial justification and should note in the negotiation record that the asymmetry was conceded.
Line 151: **Walk-away:** Any Seller Margin Threshold below \$500,000 is not acceptable without escalation. A Seller Margin Threshold of less than \$500,000 --- and in particular, thresholds of \$250,000 or less for Seller deliveries --- would subject Meridian to frequent small-value margin calls that impose disproportionate operational burden on Meridian\'s New York--based operations and settlement teams. The operational cost of processing and settling margin calls at low thresholds (including settlement instruction preparation, DTC or Clearstream delivery execution, and internal booking and reconciliation) can be significant in aggregate, particularly across a large portfolio of outstanding Transactions with a single counterparty. If a counterparty insists on a Seller Margin Threshold below \$500,000, the desk must escalate per Section 9.
Line 165: > \(e\) **Valuation methodology:** Market Value for margin purposes must be determined by reference to closing bid-side prices from a recognized pricing source (Bloomberg or Reuters) on the business day immediately preceding the margin call date. Mid-market pricing or offer-side pricing is not acceptable. Where the counterparty proposes an alternative valuation methodology, the desk should insist on bid-side pricing (which is more conservative from the Seller\'s perspective, as it results in a lower Market Value and therefore a lower likelihood of Meridian being required to deliver margin) or escalate to Risk Management if the alternative methodology could materially affect margin call frequency or magnitude.
Line 189: > \(c\) No prior consent of Buyer is required. This is a critical element of the acceptable formulation. The distinction between a substitution right that is subject to conditions (acceptable) and a substitution right that requires Buyer consent (not acceptable) is fundamental. A conditional substitution right preserves Meridian\'s control over the timing and execution of the substitution; a consent-based substitution right transfers that control to the Buyer and introduces the risk of delay or refusal, which is operationally unacceptable.
Line 191: **Walk-away:** Any requirement for Buyer\'s prior written consent to substitution is unacceptable. Such a provision effectively converts the repo into a pledge structure from an operational perspective, even if the legal characterization as a sale and repurchase is preserved. If the Buyer must consent before Meridian can substitute collateral, Meridian\'s collateral management team cannot reliably plan or execute portfolio rebalancing, and the practical utility of the substitution right is severely impaired. The desk must not agree to a consent requirement under any circumstances without escalation to the Managing Director and the General Counsel under the walk-away override procedures described in Section 9.3.
Line 193: If a counterparty insists on consent rights, the desk should explain that the \"same-or-better\" collateral quality condition and the \"no Margin Deficit\" condition described above adequately protect the Buyer\'s interests. The Buyer\'s credit exposure is unaffected by a substitution that delivers collateral of equivalent or better quality and value, and the Buyer\'s protection against undercollateralization is preserved by the no-Margin-Deficit condition. Consent mechanisms introduce unacceptable operational delay --- particularly in cross-border transactions where the Buyer\'s credit and operations teams may be in different time zones from Meridian\'s operations desk --- and serve no legitimate protective function that is not already addressed by the two conditions described above.
Line 199: > \(a\) European bank counterparties commonly open by requiring Buyer\'s prior written consent to any substitution. This is a standard opening position in European bank playbooks and should not be treated as a walk-away trigger for the negotiation as a whole. Instead, the desk should counter with the acceptable formulation described in Section 5.1 (conditional substitution without consent) and explain the commercial rationale. In the experience of the desk, most European bank counterparties will ultimately accept the conditional formulation after one or two rounds of negotiation.
Line 203: > \(c\) The 1 business day notice period is operationally critical. It provides Meridian\'s operations team with sufficient lead time to coordinate with the relevant settlement systems --- The Depository Trust Company (\"DTC\") for USD-denominated collateral and Clearstream Banking S.A. for EUR-denominated collateral --- to prepare and execute the simultaneous delivery of substitute collateral and receipt of original collateral. A shorter notice period (e.g., same-day notice) may not provide adequate time for settlement instruction preparation and execution, particularly for EUR-denominated collateral settling through Clearstream, which operates on Central European Time. A longer notice period (e.g., 2 or more business days) may be acceptable if the counterparty insists but reduces Meridian\'s agility in managing its collateral book and should not be offered proactively.
Line 209: Repricing provisions allow one or both parties to adjust the Purchase Price of an outstanding Transaction to reflect changes in the Market Value of the Purchased Securities or changes in prevailing market repo rates during the Transaction\'s term. From Meridian\'s perspective as Seller, in-term repricing introduces operational complexity and potential P&L volatility, particularly where repricing triggers a cash payment obligation (either a payment by Meridian to the counterparty if the Market Value of the collateral has declined, or a return of cash by the counterparty to Meridian if the Market Value has increased). The desk\'s objective is to minimize repricing frequency while acknowledging that bank counterparties with term repo exposures have a legitimate interest in periodic repricing to manage their balance-sheet exposure.
Line 213: **Target:** Repricing available only at maturity roll --- that is, no in-term repricing right for either party during the life of an individual Transaction. Under this formulation, the Purchase Price set at the inception of a Transaction would remain fixed throughout the Transaction\'s term, and any adjustment to pricing would occur only when the Transaction matures and is rolled into a new Transaction (if applicable). This target position eliminates the operational burden of in-term repricing and provides Meridian with pricing certainty for the duration of each Transaction.
Line 215: **Acceptable:** Quarterly repricing or repricing on the 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date, whichever occurs later, with no less than 2 business days\' prior written notice by the requesting party. The desk may agree to either a quarterly cycle (i.e., repricing on the 91st, 182nd, and 273rd calendar day from the Purchase Date, or the next business day if such date falls on a non-business day) or a 90-day cycle (i.e., repricing on each 90th calendar day from the Purchase Date). Where the counterparty proposes both triggers --- for example, repricing on each calendar quarter-end *and* on each 90th calendar day --- the \"whichever is later\" formulation ensures that Meridian is not subject to repricing more frequently than quarterly. The desk should insist on this qualifier in all cases where both triggers are proposed.
Line 217: The 2 business day notice period is a critical element of the acceptable formulation. It provides Meridian\'s operations team with adequate time to source replacement collateral, adjust positions, prepare cash for any repricing payment, and coordinate with settlement systems. The 2 business day period also allows for at least one full business day of internal processing after receipt of the repricing notice, accounting for the possibility that the notice is received near end-of-day.
Line 219: **Walk-away:** Any repricing frequency more often than quarterly --- including but not limited to monthly repricing, bi-weekly repricing, weekly repricing, or on-demand repricing at the counterparty\'s sole discretion --- is not acceptable. In-term repricing at sub-quarterly frequency imposes significant operational and P&L volatility on the desk and is disproportionate to the counterparty\'s legitimate risk management needs. Sub-quarterly repricing must be escalated under the walk-away procedures described in Section 9, and approval is expected to be granted only in extraordinary circumstances (e.g., a transaction with an unusually long tenor and unusual collateral characteristics that justify more frequent adjustments).
Line 225: > \(a\) Bank counterparties conducting term trades in excess of 60 calendar days will uniformly resist Meridian\'s target of repricing only at maturity roll. The desk should expect to concede this point early in the negotiation and move promptly to the acceptable position. Protracted insistence on the \"repricing at maturity only\" target in the face of clear counterparty resistance is unlikely to be productive and may consume negotiation capital that is better deployed on other issues.
Line 227: > \(b\) The critical protection for Meridian in the acceptable position nst its net capital computation in connection with close-out or unwind scenarios; and
Line 253: > \(d\) The desk\'s recommendation, including any proposed conditions or mitigants (e.g., a higher threshold that applies only to Meridian\'s obligations, or a cure period that applies before the Cross-Default is triggered).
Line 255: **Walk-away:** Any cross-default threshold below \$15,000,000 is not acceptable under any circumstances. At \$15,000,000, the threshold would represent less than 3.64% of Meridian\'s audited net capital --- a level at which routine mark-to-market losses, minor operational payment failures, or ordinary-course settlement disputes could trigger cascading defaults across Meridian\'s agreement portfolio. The systemic risk to Meridian of a low cross-default threshold is disproportionate to the incremental credit protection it provides to the counterparty, particularly given that the counterparty\'s primary protection in a repo transaction is the collateral itself, supplemented by margin provisions. Negotiators must not agree to a cross-default threshold below \$15,000,000 even with escalation; this is a hard walk-away, and no override is available. If a counterparty refuses to accept a threshold at or above \$15,000,000, the desk should inform the General Counsel and the Managing Director, and the negotiation should be paused pending a senior-level commercial discussion about whether the counterparty relationship can proceed on other terms.
Line 257: **7.2 --- Cross-Default Negotiation Notes**
Line 261: > \(a\) European bank counterparties with large CET1 capital bases --- for example, Voss Bank AG, which reported CET1 of CHF 8,300,000,000 as of 31 December 2024 --- routinely propose low cross-default thresholds, often in the range of \$10,000,000 to \$15,000,000. The rationale cited by such counterparties is that these amounts are immaterial relative to their own balance sheets and that their standard credit playbooks require low thresholds for non-bank counterparties. The desk should explain to such counterparties that the cross-default threshold must be calibrated to Meridian\'s capital base, not the counterparty\'s. A \$10,000,000 threshold that is immaterial to a bank with CHF 8,300,000,000 in CET1 capital is manifestly not immaterial to a broker-dealer with \$412,000,000 in net capital, and the cascading-default risk of a \$10,000,000 threshold is borne entirely by Meridian. This is a straightforward and well-understood argument, and most European bank counterparties will accept it when presented clearly and early in the negotiation.
Line 263: > \(b\) Offer the \$25,000,000 midpoint as a compromise early in the negotiation to avoid protracted discussion on this issue. Cross-default threshold negotiations can consume disproportionate time and attention relative to their commercial significance, and the desk is better served by closing on this point quickly at \$25,000,000 and reserving its negotiation capital for issues such as substitution rights and repricing.
Line 265: > \(c\) The desk should be alert to counterparty proposals that define \"indebtedness\" broadly for purposes of the Cross-Default provision --- for example, proposals that include trade payables, margin obligations under other agreements, or contingent liabilities (such as guarantees) within the definition of \"indebtedness.\" The desk should resist such expansive definitions and should insist that \"indebtedness\" for Cross-Default purposes be limited to borrowed money and debt securities, which is the standard GMRA formulation. An expansive definition of \"indebtedness\" effectively lowers the functional cross-default threshold by increasing the universe of obligations that can trigger the provision.
Line 267: > \(d\) Where the counterparty proposes a \"cross-acceleration\" provision rather than a true \"cross-default\" provision, the desk may consider this as a more favorable alternative, as cross-acceleration requires not merely a default under the other agreement but an actual acceleration of the obligations under that agreement. Cross-acceleration provides the counterparty with less aggressive protection than cross-default (because a default may exist for some time before acceleration occurs), but it is commercially reasonable and reduces the risk of cascading defaults triggered by technical or curable defaults. The desk may offer cross-acceleration as a compromise if the counterparty resists the \$25,000,000 cross-default threshold.
Line 269: **7.3 --- Act of Insolvency Grace Period**
Line 271: The Act of Insolvency provision in a GMRA or MRA provides that the occurrence of certain insolvency-related events --- including the filing of a bankruptcy petition (whether voluntary or involuntary), the appointment of a receiver or liquidator, the making of an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or the admission in writing of an inability to pay debts as they come due --- constitutes an Event of Default. The key negotiation issue is whether the Act of Insolvency Event of Default is triggered immediately upon the occurrence of the insolvency event or whether the affected party is entitled to a grace period to cure the event before it ripens into an Event of Default.
Line 273: **Target:** 30 calendar days\' grace period for curing an Act of Insolvency. Under this formulation, the occurrence of an insolvency-related event does not constitute an immediate Event of Default if the event is cured, dismissed, or vacated within 30 calendar days. A 30-calendar-day grace period provides Meridian with substantial time to respond to an involuntary bankruptcy petition (which may be frivolous or unfounded), to correct an administrative error in a regulatory filing, or to take other appropriate action to resolve the insolvency event. This target is aggressive and is unlikely to be accepted by most bank counterparties without significant concession, but it establishes a strong opening position.
Line 275: **Acceptable:** 10 to 15 business days. The desk may agree to any grace period within this range without escalation.
