27: Right-click to update Table of Contents
28: 
29: **[Section 1 --- Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**
30: 
31: **[1.1 --- Purpose]{.underline}**
32: 
33: This playbook sets out Voss Bank AG\'s standard negotiation positions, approved fallback positions, and absolute walk-away thresholds for the negotiation of Global Master Repurchase Agreements under the 2011 ICMA form (with 2011 Annex I). It is intended to equip the Collateral Trading & Legal team at the London Branch (FCA FRN 487203) with authoritative guidance for each material commercial and legal term, enabling front-to-back consistency across all repo and reverse repo negotiations and ensuring that all agreed terms remain within parameters approved by the Credit Committee in Zürich.
34: 
35: The playbook serves several core functions. First, it provides the desk with a single, comprehensive reference document that eliminates the need for ad hoc consultation on routine negotiation points. Second, it establishes a clear escalation framework so that the desk and Legal know precisely when a counterparty proposal exceeds the authority delegated to the London Branch and must be referred to the Credit Committee. Third, it promotes institutional consistency --- ensuring that materially similar counterparties receive materially similar terms, and that departures from standard terms are documented and justified. Fourth, it reduces the risk of inadvertent agreement to terms that are incompatible with Voss Bank\'s regulatory obligations, including under FINMA\'s liquidity, capital, and large-exposure frameworks.
36: 
37: The following principles govern the application of this playbook:
38: 
39: > • This playbook is applicable to all GMRA negotiations conducted by or on behalf of Voss Bank AG, London Branch (LEI: 2138004WJZ83NHQKF744; CHE-314.827.059). For the avoidance of doubt, this includes negotiations where the London Branch acts through its appointed external counsel, Calder Stone Partners LLP, or through any other authorised legal adviser.
40: >
41: > • This playbook is not legal advice and does not override Credit Committee mandates issued on a counterparty-specific basis. Where a Credit Committee mandate imposes terms that differ from those set out in this playbook, the Credit Committee mandate prevails. The desk should annotate the relevant sections of this playbook to reflect any counterparty-specific mandates in effect.
42: >
43: > • Where a counterparty\'s regulatory status (e.g., SEC-registered broker-dealer, PRA/FCA-authorised firm, CFTC-registered swap dealer) creates specific structural requirements --- for example, with respect to the treatment of customer property under the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA), or with respect to margin segregation requirements under FCA CASS rules --- the desk must consult Calder Stone Partners LLP or internal Legal before deviating from the playbook positions stated herein. Regulatory-driven structural requirements may necessitate bespoke provisions that fall outside the standard terms addressed in this document.
44: >
45: > • Nothing in this playbook limits or modifies the obligation of the desk to comply with Voss Bank AG\'s broader compliance policies, including the Anti-Money Laundering and Sanctions Policy, the Market Abuse Policy, and the Conflicts of Interest Policy, each as in effect from time to time.
46: 
47: **[1.2 --- Scope of Application]{.underline}**
48: 
49: This playbook applies to the following instruments, structures, and settlement arrangements:
50: 
51: > • **2011 ICMA GMRA and Annex I elections.** The 2011 form is Voss Bank\'s standard master agreement for repurchase transactions. Voss Bank does not, as a matter of policy, negotiate under the 1995 ICMA GMRA or the 2000 TBMA/ISMA GMRA. If a counterparty proposes either legacy form, the desk should insist on migrating to the 2011 form. If the counterparty refuses, escalate to Legal.
52: >
53: > • **Bilateral and tri-party repo and reverse repo.** The playbook covers both bilateral structures (where collateral moves directly between the parties\' custodians or settlement accounts) and tri-party structures (including where BNY Meliora Trust Company, N.A. is appointed as tri-party custodian). The default structure under this playbook is bilateral; tri-party is elected only where specifically agreed and documented via a separate tri-party annexe.
54: >
55: > • **Buy/Sell Back transactions only where the Buy/Sell Back Annex is separately elected.** Buy/Sell Back treatment is not the default under this playbook. Where a counterparty specifically requests Buy/Sell Back treatment --- for example, to accommodate back-office systems that process Buy/Sell Back confirmations rather than classic repo confirmations --- the desk must refer the matter to Legal for negotiation of a separate Buy/Sell Back Annex. The desk should not agree to Buy/Sell Back treatment as part of the standard Annex I elections.
56: >
57: > • **Settlement through Clearstream Banking S.A.** (for Euro-denominated Eligible Collateral) **and The Depository Trust Company** (for USD-denominated Eligible Collateral). These are the standard settlement systems for the London Branch. Alternative settlement systems may be considered on a case-by-case basis, but any departure from these standard elections requires discussion with Operations (London) to confirm settlement capability.
58: 
59: **[1.3 --- How to Use This Playbook]{.underline}**
60: 
61: Each section below addresses a material commercial or legal term that arises in a typical GMRA negotiation. For each term, the playbook identifies three tiers of positioning:
62: 
63: > • **Preferred Position** --- the opening term Voss Bank will propose in a Turn 1 draft. This is the position that appears in Voss Bank\'s standard-form Annex I or in the initial mark-up of the counterparty\'s draft (where the counterparty circulates the first draft). The preferred position represents Voss Bank\'s optimal commercial and risk outcome. It is the starting point for all negotiations, and the desk should not concede the preferred position without first testing the counterparty\'s willingness to accept it.
64: >
65: > • **Fallback / Acceptable Range** --- the range of compromise the desk and Legal may agree without escalation to the Credit Committee. Within this range, the desk lead (at Director level) has full authority to agree terms on behalf of Voss Bank. The acceptable range is calibrated to reflect credit, regulatory, and market considerations, and to allow the desk sufficient flexibility to reach commercial agreement with a reasonable counterparty. Where the acceptable range is expressed as a numeric band (e.g., \$10,000,000 to \$25,000,000), any figure within the band --- including the endpoints --- may be agreed without escalation.
66: >
67: > • **Walk-Away Threshold** --- the point beyond which the term is unacceptable. Any counterparty proposal at or beyond this threshold requires escalation to the Credit Committee under Section 12 of this playbook. In certain cases, the walk-away threshold is absolute --- meaning that the Credit Committee itself is not authorised to approve a term beyond that point, and Voss Bank must either negotiate the counterparty away from its position or decline the transaction. In other cases, the walk-away threshold triggers a mandatory escalation, but the Credit Committee retains discretion to approve the term under exceptional circumstances.
68: 
69: The playbook also includes practical illustrations drawn from current or recent negotiations, particularly the ongoing negotiation with Meridian Capital Securities LLC (see Section 17 for a comprehensive counterparty-specific summary). These illustrations are intended to demonstrate how the playbook positions translate into real-world negotiation dynamics. They should not be treated as precedent for future negotiations with different counterparties, except to the extent that the underlying principles are of general application.
70: 
71: **[1.4 --- Current Active Negotiations]{.underline}**
72: 
73: This version of the playbook (Version 3.1) incorporates lessons from, and provides guidance specific to, the ongoing negotiation with **Meridian Capital Securities LLC** (CRD# 298417; EIN 83-2947561; LEI: 5493007XKBT49LP2QR12), a Delaware-organised SEC-registered broker-dealer. Meridian is a mid-tier US broker-dealer with a diversified secured funding business and an audited net capital of \$412,000,000 as at 31 December 2024.
74: 
75: The Meridian negotiation is at Turn 3 stage. Voss Bank circulated its Turn 1 draft on 14 March 2025. Meridian returned its Turn 2 redline on 28 March 2025, raising 23 individual mark-ups across the GMRA and Annex I. Of those 23 marks, 16 were non-commercial drafting changes and 7 were substantive commercial or legal proposals. Alistair Fenn of Calder Stone Partners LLP responded to 14 of the 23 marks by email on 4 April 2025, accepting 7 and providing Voss Bank\'s counter-position on the remaining 7. A call between Dana R. Castellano (Meridian\'s lead negotiator) and Henrik J. Lindqvist on 11 April 2025 resolved three of the outstanding commercial issues (sovereign haircut, corporate haircut, and margin threshold). Rachel S. Okonkwo of Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP (PAG) memorialised the call resolutions by email on 14 April 2025. Meridian\'s Turn 3 redline and updated issues list are due from PAG on 18 April 2025.
76: 
77: References to the Meridian negotiation are included as practical illustrations throughout this playbook. The counterparty-specific terms, issues tracker, and Annex I elections summary for Meridian are consolidated in Section 17.
78: 
79: **[Section 2 --- Base Currency, Transaction Types, and Netting]{.underline}**
80: 
81: **[2.1 --- Base Currency]{.underline}**
82: 
83: The Base Currency for all GMRA negotiations conducted by the London Branch is **USD**. This is both the preferred and the mandatory election. The desk does not have authority to agree a Base Currency other than USD without Credit Committee approval.
84: 
85: All haircut calculations, margin thresholds, exposure caps, cross-default thresholds, and any other monetary amounts specified in the GMRA or Annex I are denominated in USD unless otherwise stated. Where a Transaction involves non-USD Purchased Securities (e.g., Euro-denominated sovereign bonds), the relevant amounts are converted to USD at the applicable spot rate for the purposes of margin calculations, exposure monitoring, and threshold comparisons.
86: 
87: The selection of USD as the mandatory Base Currency reflects the London Branch\'s primary funding activities in USD-denominated repo markets and ensures consistency with the Branch\'s internal risk management systems, which are calibrated to USD exposures.
88: 
89: **[2.2 --- Buy/Sell Back Transactions]{.underline}**
90: 
91: The default election for Buy/Sell Back Transactions under the GMRA is **Not Applicable**. This means that the Buy/Sell Back Annex (ICMA form) is not incorporated into the GMRA as a default matter, and no Transaction entered into under the GMRA will be treated as a Buy/Sell Back Transaction unless the parties have separately agreed and executed a Buy/Sell Back Annex.
92: 
93: Where a counterparty requests Buy/Sell Back treatment --- for example, because the counterparty\'s back-office systems are configured to process Buy/Sell Back confirmations, or because the counterparty\'s internal legal framework treats Buy/Sell Back Transactions differently from classic repos for tax or accounting purposes --- the desk must escalate to Legal. Legal will assess whether the Buy/Sell Back Annex can be incorporated without adverse effects on Voss Bank\'s netting, HQLA, or capital treatment, and will negotiate any necessary amendments to the standard Buy/Sell Back Annex.
94: 
95: The desk should not agree to Buy/Sell Back treatment as a standard Annex I election. The structural differences between classic repo and Buy/Sell Back --- particularly with respect to the treatment of income payments and the mechanics of close-out --- warrant separate and careful consideration.
96: 
97: **[2.3 --- Agency Transactions]{.underline}**
98: 
99: The default election for Agency Transactions is **Not Applicable**. Voss Bank AG, London Branch, transacts solely as principal in all repo and reverse repo transactions. The London Branch does not act as agent for any other entity, and it does not accept counterparties acting in an agency capacity unless the underlying principal is separately identified, credit-approved, and documented.
100: 
101: If a counterparty proposes that it will act as agent for an undisclosed or disclosed principal, the desk must immediately escalate to Legal and the Credit Committee. Agency structures introduce additional credit, legal, and regulatory risks, including questions of counterparty identification for AML/KYC purposes, the applicability of close-out netting opinions, and the treatment of the agency relationship under SIPA (for US broker-dealers) or the FCA\'s client asset rules (for UK-authorised firms).
102: 
103: **[2.4 --- Netting]{.underline}**
104: 
105: Voss Bank\'s preferred election is that **Paragraph 7(b) of the GMRA is elected**. Paragraph 7(b) provides for the netting of payment obligations arising under Transactions on the same settlement date and in the same currency. This netting mechanism reduces settlement risk by minimising the number and gross value of payment flows between the parties on any given day.
106: 
107: Netting applies on a **same-currency, same-settlement-date basis** only. The desk must resist any counterparty attempt to broaden the netting scope to include cross-currency netting (i.e., netting of payment obligations denominated in different currencies) or cross-settlement-date netting (i.e., netting of payment obligations falling due on different settlement dates). Cross-currency and cross-settlement-date netting introduce additional complexities, including FX conversion risk, timing mismatch risk, and potential inconsistencies with close-out netting opinions. Any proposal to broaden netting beyond the same-currency, same-settlement-date framework requires Credit Committee approval.
108: 
109: For the avoidance of doubt, the netting election under Paragraph 7(b) is distinct from the close-out netting provisions that apply upon an Event of Default or termination of the GMRA. Close-out netting is addressed in the body of the GMRA (Paragraph 10) and is not subject to election under Annex I. The enforceability of close-out netting is addressed in Section 15.1 of this playbook.
110: 
111: **[Section 3 --- Haircuts by Collateral Type]{.underline}**
112: 
113: Haircuts are among the most commercially significant terms in any GMRA negotiation. The haircut determines the relationship between the Market Value of the Purchased Securities and the Purchase Price, and thereby establishes the degree of overcollateralisation that protects Voss Bank (as Buyer) against a decline in the value of the collateral between margin call dates. Haircuts also have direct regulatory consequences: haircuts that are too low may cause received collateral to fall below the thresholds required for HQLA classification or may result in higher capital charges under the Basel III standardised approach for securities financing transactions.
114: 
115: The haircuts set out below apply to the initial calculation of Purchase Price. They are not intended to replace or limit the ongoing margin maintenance provisions of the GMRA (including the Margin Ratio, if separately agreed), but rather to establish the baseline overcollateralisation at the inception of each Transaction.
116: 
117: **[3.1 --- Sovereign Collateral]{.underline}**
118: 
119:   -----------------------------------------------------------------------
120:   **Parameter**                       **Position**
121:   ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
122:   **Preferred Haircut**               **2.0%**
123: 
124:   **Minimum Acceptable**              **1.5%**
125: 
126:   **Walk-Away**                       Below 1.5%
127:   -----------------------------------------------------------------------
128: 
129: **Eligible Sovereign Issuers.** Sovereign collateral is limited to obligations of G7 nations only --- that is, the United States of America, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, the Federal Republic of Germany, the French Republic, Japan, Canada, and the Italian Republic. Obligations of sub-sovereign issuers (e.g., US states or municipalities, German Länder, Canadian provinces) are not eligible as sovereign collateral for the purposes of this playbook, even where such obligations carry an explicit sovereign guarantee. Sub-sovereign obligations may be considered as a separate collateral category on a case-by-case basis, subject to Credit Committee approval.
130: 
131: **Minimum Credit Quality.** Eligible sovereign obligations must be rated **A--** (S&P Global Ratings) / **A3** (Moody\'s Investors Service) or better by at least one of those two agencies at the time of the relevant Transaction and continuously thereafter. If a sovereign issuer\'s credit rating falls below A-- / A3 during the term of a Transaction, the affected Purchased Securities cease to qualify as Eligible Collateral and must be substituted or the Transaction must be repriced. This requirement is implemented through the standard Eligible Collateral definition in Annex I, supplemented by Voss Bank\'s standard ratings-downgrade trigger clause.
132: 
133: **Haircut Application and Illustrative Calculations.** The haircut is applied as a discount to Market Value to determine the Purchase Price. Specifically, the Purchase Price is calculated as the Market Value of the Purchased Securities divided by one plus the applicable haircut percentage (expressed as a decimal). This methodology ensures that the haircut operates as a true overcollateralisation buffer --- the Seller delivers securities with a Market Value that exceeds the cash advanced by the Buyer by the haircut percentage.
134: 
135: At the preferred 2.0% haircut, illustrative sovereign collateral with a Market Value of \$100,000,000 produces a Purchase Price of **\$98,039,215.69** (\$100,000,000 ÷ 1.02). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,960,784.31, representing 2.0% of the Purchase Price.
136: 
137: At the minimum acceptable 1.5% haircut, the same collateral would produce a Purchase Price of **\$98,522,167.49** (\$100,000,000 ÷ 1.015). The overcollateralisation buffer narrows to \$1,477,832.51, representing 1.5% of the Purchase Price.
138: 
139: **Negotiation Dynamics.** For current negotiations (e.g., the Meridian negotiation), a midpoint of **1.75%** is within acceptable parameters and may be offered in a Turn 3 or later round as a commercial concession if the counterparty has proposed 1.5% and Voss Bank has opened at 2.0%. At the 1.75% midpoint, \$100,000,000 Market Value yields a Purchase Price of **\$98,280,098.28**, and the overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,719,901.72.
140: 
141: The desk should be aware that sovereign haircuts below 2.0% are increasingly common in the interdealer market for G7 sovereign collateral, particularly for US Treasury securities and German Bunds. The preferred 2.0% position may meet resistance from sophisticated counterparties, and the desk should be prepared to move to the midpoint range relatively early in the negotiation in exchange for concessions on other commercial terms (e.g., margin threshold, cross-default threshold, or repricing frequency).
142: 
143: **[3.2 --- Corporate Collateral]{.underline}**
144: 
145:   -----------------------------------------------------------------------
146:   **Parameter**                       **Position**
147:   ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
148:   **Preferred Haircut**               **5.0%**
149: 
150:   **Minimum Acceptable**              **4.0%**
151: 
152:   **Walk-Away**                       Below 3.5%
153:   -----------------------------------------------------------------------
154: 
155: **Eligible Corporate Bonds.** Eligible corporate collateral consists of corporate bonds rated **BBB+** (S&P Global Ratings) / **Baa1** (Moody\'s Investors Service) or better, with a residual maturity of **10 years or less** at the time of the relevant Transaction. Bonds with a residual maturity exceeding 10 years are excluded due to their higher duration risk and greater sensitivity to interest rate movements, which increases the probability of a material decline in Market Value between margin call dates.
156: 
157: Convertible bonds, contingent convertible bonds (CoCos), subordinated debt instruments, and any instrument with equity-linked features are excluded from the definition of Eligible Corporate Collateral regardless of credit rating or residual maturity. The desk should be vigilant for counterparty proposals that seek to broaden the definition of Eligible Corporate Collateral to include any such instruments.
158: 
159: **Haircut Application and Illustrative Calculations.** At the preferred 5.0% haircut, illustrative corporate collateral with a Market Value of \$50,000,000 produces a Purchase Price of **\$47,619,047.62** (\$50,000,000 ÷ 1.05). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$2,380,952.38.
160: 
161: At the minimum acceptable 4.0% haircut, the Purchase Price would be **\$48,076,923.08** (\$50,000,000 ÷ 1.04). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,923,076.92.
162: 
163: A counterparty counter of 3.5% sits at the extreme low end of Voss Bank\'s tolerance. The midpoint of 5.0% and 3.5% --- i.e., **4.25%** --- falls within the acceptable range and may be agreed without escalation. At 4.25%, \$50,000,000 Market Value yields a Purchase Price of **\$47,961,630.70**, and the overcollateralisation buffer is \$2,038,369.30.
164: 
165: **Walk-Away.** Haircuts below 3.5% are outside the acceptable range and constitute a walk-away unless the Credit Committee grants a specific counterparty exception pursuant to the escalation procedures set out in Section 12. The desk should note, however, that haircuts in the range of 3.5% to 4.0% fall within a \"grey zone\" --- they are technically within the walk-away boundary but below the minimum acceptable threshold. Any counterparty proposal in this grey zone must be escalated to the Credit Committee before agreement.
166: 
167: **[3.3 --- HQLA Eligibility Note]{.underline}**
168: 
169: The haircut levels set out in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 are calibrated to ensure that reverse repo collateral continues to qualify as Level 1 (sovereign) or Level 2A (eligible corporate) High-Quality Liquid Assets under the FINMA Liquidity Ordinance (LiqV) and the CRR delegated acts as applied via the Swiss \"equivalence\" framework. Maintenance of HQLA eligibility is critical to Voss Bank\'s compliance with the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirements imposed by FINMA.
170: 
171: The desk must not agree haircuts that would cause received collateral to fall below HQLA eligibility thresholds as periodically published by Treasury (Zürich). As of the date of this playbook, the current HQLA-floor haircuts are as follows:
172: 
173: > • **Level 1 sovereign collateral:** 0.5% minimum haircut.
174: >
175: > • **Level 2A corporate collateral:** 3.0% minimum haircut.
176: 
177: These floors represent the absolute regulatory minimum. The preferred and minimum acceptable haircuts stated in this playbook are intentionally set well above the HQLA floors to provide a margin of safety against regulatory reclassification. If a counterparty proposes haircuts that approach the HQLA floors --- even if the proposed haircut remains above the floor --- the desk must consult Treasury (Zürich) to confirm that the proposed level does not create adverse LCR or NSFR consequences.
178: 
179: Treasury (Zürich) updates the HQLA-floor haircuts at least semi-annually, or more frequently if there are material changes to the FINMA framework or to the CRR delegated acts. The desk should check the most recent Treasury circular before finalising haircut terms in any negotiation.
180: 
181: **[Section 4 --- Margin Thresholds]{.underline}**
182: 
183: The Margin Threshold determines the minimum aggregate Margin Deficit or Margin Excess that must exist before either party is obligated to make or entitled to receive a margin transfer. A well-calibrated Margin Threshold reduces the operational burden of frequent small margin calls while ensuring that material exposure imbalances are promptly addressed. The Margin Threshold is distinct from the haircut (which establishes the initial overcollateralisation) and from the Net Exposure Cap (which limits the aggregate credit exposure to a single counterparty).
184: 
185: **[4.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**
186: 
187: Voss Bank\'s preferred Margin Threshold is **\$250,000 symmetric** --- that is, the same threshold applies to margin calls made by either party (Buyer or Seller), and no transfer of Margin Securities or Cash Margin is required unless the aggregate Margin Deficit or Margin Excess, as applicable, exceeds \$250,000. This threshold is applied on an aggregate, cross-Transaction basis (i.e., it is calculated with reference to the net margin position across all outstanding Transactions under the GMRA, not on a Transaction-by-Transaction basis).
188: 
189: The \$250,000 symmetric threshold is appropriate for the majority of Voss Bank\'s counterparties. It strikes a balance between operational efficiency (avoiding de minimis margin calls that consume settlement capacity without meaningfully reducing credit exposure) and risk management (ensuring that margin calls are triggered before exposure becomes material relative to the haircut buffer).
190: 
191: **[4.2 --- Acceptable Fallback --- Asymmetric Thresholds]{.underline}**
192: 
193: Where a counterparty (e.g., a regulated broker-dealer with net capital constraints, or a central bank with operational limitations on daily margin transfers) insists on a higher threshold for its own margin delivery obligations, Voss Bank may accept an **asymmetric** threshold structure. Under an asymmetric structure, the Margin Threshold for margin calls made by one party differs from the threshold for margin calls made by the other party.
194: 
195: Specifically, Voss Bank is prepared to accept the following asymmetric arrangement:
196: 
197: > • **Margin Threshold for Seller (counterparty) deliveries: up to \$500,000** --- acceptable provided that the **Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold remains at \$250,000**. Under this structure, the counterparty (as Seller) is not obligated to deliver Margin Securities or Cash Margin unless the aggregate Margin Deficit exceeds \$500,000, whereas Voss Bank (as Buyer) must return excess margin if the aggregate Margin Excess exceeds \$250,000.
198: >
199: > • This structure recognises that the counterparty bears a higher margining burden as Seller (because it is the party delivering margin in response to a margin deficit) while Voss Bank retains the benefit of a lower call threshold as Buyer (meaning that Voss Bank can call for margin at the \$250,000 level even though the counterparty cannot call for return of excess margin until the \$500,000 level is reached).
200: 
201: In the current Meridian negotiation, Meridian proposed \$500,000 symmetric at Turn 2. The acceptable resolution --- communicated to Meridian by Henrik J. Lindqvist on the 11 April 2025 call --- is to concede \$500,000 on Seller (Meridian) deliveries while holding the Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold at \$250,000. This outcome is within the desk\'s delegated authority and does not require Credit Committee approval.
202: 
203: **[4.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**
204: 
205: The following positions are at or beyond the walk-away threshold:
206: 
207: > • Any threshold above **\$500,000** for either party requires Credit Committee approval. The desk does not have authority to agree a Margin Threshold in excess of \$500,000 for either the Buyer or the Seller.
208: >
209: > • Any proposal to raise the Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold above \$250,000 is presumptively unacceptable absent exceptional credit quality of the counterparty (e.g., a sovereign wealth fund or central bank with a AAA credit rating). Raising the Buyer threshold above \$250,000 reduces Voss Bank\'s ability to call for margin promptly and increases the risk that a material margin deficit will accumulate before a call can be made.
210: >
211: > • Any proposal to eliminate the Margin Threshold entirely (i.e., to set the threshold at zero) should be viewed with caution, even though it is ostensibly more protective of Voss Bank\'s interests. A zero threshold creates significant operational burden and may result in a high volume of de minimis margin calls that strain settlement capacity. If a counterparty proposes a zero threshold, the desk should propose \$250,000 symmetric as a more practical alternative.
212: 
213: **[4.4 --- Margin Call Mechanics]{.underline}**
214: 
215: In addition to the Margin Threshold, the following margin call mechanics are standard Annex I elections and should be included in all GMRA negotiations:
216: 
217: > • **Margin call cut-off time: 10:00 a.m. London time.** This is the time by which a margin call must be received by the recipient party in order to trigger a same-day settlement obligation.
218: >
219: > • **Calls received before cut-off: same-day settlement.** If a valid margin call is received before 10:00 a.m. London time on a business day, the responding party must deliver the required Margin Securities or Cash Margin on the same business day.
220: >
221: > • **Calls received at or after cut-off: next business day settlement.** If a valid margin call is received at or after 10:00 a.m. London time, the responding party\'s obligation to deliver Margin Securities or Cash Margin is deferred to the next business day.
222: 
223: The 10:00 a.m. London time cut-off is non-negotiable. It aligns with the London Branch\'s operational cycle and with the settlement windows of the Branch\'s primary settlement systems (Clearstream and DTC). Counterparty proposals to move the cut-off to a later time (e.g., 12:00 noon London time or 10:00 a.m. New York time) should be resisted. If the counterparty insists on a later cut-off, consult Operations (London) to confirm whether a later cut-off can be operationally accommodated before making any concession.
224: 
225: **[Section 5 --- Net Exposure Cap]{.underline}**
226: 
227: **[5.1 --- Standard Cap]{.underline}**
228: 
229: The Net Exposure Cap is the maximum aggregate net credit exposure that Voss Bank is prepared to accept to a single counterparty under the GMRA. It is set on a counterparty-by-counterparty basis by the Credit Committee in Zürich, based on the counterparty\'s credit profile, the nature and expected volume of the trading relationship, and Voss Bank\'s overall portfolio concentration limits.
230: 
231: For the Meridian Capital Securities LLC relationship, the approved Net Exposure Cap is **\$1,500,000,000** (one billion five hundred million US dollars). This cap was approved by the Credit Committee on 7 March 2025 as part of the pre-negotiation credit approval for the Meridian GMRA.
232: 
233: The Net Exposure Cap is expressed as a single aggregate figure and is not broken down by Transaction type, collateral type, or tenor. It applies to the aggregate net mark-to-market exposure across all outstanding Transactions under the GMRA at any point in time, after giving effect to haircuts and any margin transfers.
234: 
235: **[5.2 --- Negotiation Guidance]{.underline}**
236: 
237: The Net Exposure Cap is not typically a negotiated term in the traditional sense. It is a unilateral credit limit set by Voss Bank to reflect its own credit risk appetite, and it is inserted into Annex I as a Buyer election. The counterparty is free to set its own exposure cap (if any) on its side, and Voss Bank will not object to a counterparty\'s unilateral cap unless it is so low as to render the trading relationship commercially unviable.
238: 
239: The desk should be aware of, and resist, the following counterparty proposals relating to the Net Exposure Cap:
240: 
241: > • **Bilateral cap.** Some counterparties will propose that the Net Exposure Cap be bilateral --- i.e., that it apply equally to both parties, so that neither party\'s aggregate net exposure may exceed the stated cap. This is inappropriate because the cap reflects Voss Bank\'s credit assessment of the counterparty, not a mutual assessment. A bilateral cap would constrain Voss Bank\'s ability to manage its own exposure unilaterally. The desk should reject bilateral cap proposals.
242: >
243: > • **Indexation.** Some counterparties (particularly US broker-dealers) will propose that the Net Exposure Cap be indexed to the counterparty\'s own net capital or regulatory capital ratios --- for example, that the cap be set at a fixed percentage of the counterparty\'s excess net capital under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Indexation introduces variability and unpredictability into the cap and creates a risk that the cap will decrease at precisely the time when the counterparty\'s credit quality is deteriorating (and when Voss Bank most needs the protection of a firm cap). The desk should reject indexation proposals.
244: >
245: > • **Periodic review.** The Credit Committee reviews Net Exposure Caps as part of its regular credit review cycle (typically annually, or more frequently if triggered by a credit event). The desk may agree to include language in Annex I stating that the cap is \"subject to periodic review,\" provided that such language does not create any obligation on Voss Bank to increase the cap or any right of the counterparty to request an increase.
246: 
247: **[Section 6 --- Substitution of Collateral]{.underline}**
248: 
249: **[6.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**
250: 
251: Voss Bank\'s preferred position on substitution of Purchased Securities is that the Seller\'s right to substitute collateral requires **prior written consent** of the Buyer (Voss Bank). Consent may be given or withheld in Buyer\'s sole and absolute discretion, and no obligation to act reasonably or in good faith shall apply to Buyer\'s exercise of the consent right.
252: 
253: This position ensures that Voss Bank can assess the HQLA eligibility, haircut adequacy, and concentration limits of any proposed substitute collateral before the substitution takes effect. It also preserves Voss Bank\'s ability to refuse substitution at times of market stress, when the quality and liquidity of substitute collateral may be difficult to assess in real time.
254: 
255: The desk should propose the prior-consent position in all Turn 1 drafts. Counterparties with active collateral management programmes will frequently resist this position, arguing that the consent requirement impedes their ability to optimise their collateral pools. The desk should be prepared for pushback and should use the prior-consent position as a negotiating lever --- conceding it in exchange for concessions on other terms, such as haircuts or margin thresholds.
256: 
257: **[6.2 --- Acceptable Fallback]{.underline}**
258: 
259: Voss Bank may accept a **no-consent** substitution framework --- that is, a framework under which the Seller may substitute Purchased Securities without obtaining Buyer\'s prior consent --- where all of the following conditions are satisfied simultaneously:

lines.text: **[VOSS BANK AG]{.underline}**
**[GMRA NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK]{.underline}**
**Collateral Trading & Legal --- Version 3.1**
**STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL --- INTERNAL USE ONLY**
**Prepared by:** Collateral Trading & Legal, Voss Bank AG, London Branch
**Approved by:** Henrik J. Lindqvist, Director --- Collateral Trading & Legal
**Version Date:** April 2025
**Supersedes:** Version 3.0 (September 2024)
**Distribution:**
> • Collateral Trading Desk (London Branch)
> • Legal (London & Zürich)
> • Credit Committee (Zürich)

This document contains proprietary negotiation strategies, approved credit parameters, and counterparty-specific commercial information. It must not be shared with, disclosed to, or made accessible to any external party, including counterparties, counterparty counsel, regulators (except upon formal regulatory request), or any other third party. Refer to Section 19 for the full confidentiality notice.
Right-click to update Table of Contents
**[Section 1 --- Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**
**[1.1 --- Purpose]{.underline}**

This playbook sets out Voss Bank AG\'s standard negotiation positions, approved fallback positions, and absolute walk-away thresholds for the negotiation of Global Master Repurchase Agreements under the 2011 ICMA form (with 2011 Annex I). It is intended to equip the Collateral Trading & Legal team at the London Branch (FCA FRN 487203) with authoritative guidance for each material commercial and legal term, enabling front-to-back consistency across all repo and reverse repo negotiations and ensuring that all agreed terms remain within parameters approved by the Credit Committee in Zürich.

The playbook serves several core functions. First, it provides the desk with a single, comprehensive reference document that eliminates the need for ad hoc consultation on routine negotiation points. Second, it establishes a clear escalation framework so that the desk and Legal know precisely when a counterparty proposal exceeds the authority delegated to the London Branch and must be referred to the Credit Committee. Third, it promotes institutional consistency --- ensuring that materially similar counterparties receive materially similar terms, and that departures from standard terms are documented and justified. Fourth, it reduces the risk of inadvertent agreement to terms that are incompatible with Voss Bank\'s regulatory obligations, including under FINMA\'s liquidity, capital, and large-exposure frameworks.
The following principles govern the application of this playbook:

> • This playbook is applicable to all GMRA negotiations conducted by or on behalf of Voss Bank AG, London Branch (LEI: 2138004WJZ83NHQKF744; CHE-314.827.059). For the avoidance of doubt, this includes negotiations where the London Branch acts through its appointed external counsel, Calder Stone Partners LLP, or through any other authorised legal adviser.

> • This playbook is not legal advice and does not override Credit Committee mandates issued on a counterparty-specific basis. Where a Credit Committee mandate imposes terms that differ from those set out in this playbook, the Credit Committee mandate prevails. The desk should annotate the relevant sections of this playbook to reflect any counterparty-specific mandates in effect.

> • Where a counterparty\'s regulatory status (e.g., SEC-registered broker-dealer, PRA/FCA-authorised firm, CFTC-registered swap dealer) creates specific structural requirements --- for example, with respect to the treatment of customer property under the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA), or with respect to margin segregation requirements under FCA CASS rules --- the desk must consult Calder Stone Partners LLP or internal Legal before deviating from the playbook positions stated herein. Regulatory-driven structural requirements may necessitate bespoke provisions that fall outside the standard terms addressed in this document.

> • Nothing in this playbook limits or modifies the obligation of the desk to comply with Voss Bank AG\'s broader compliance policies, including the Anti-Money Laundering and Sanctions Policy, the Market Abuse Policy, and the Conflicts of Interest Policy, each as in effect from time to time.
**[1.2 --- Scope of Application]{.underline}**
This playbook applies to the following instruments, structures, and settlement arrangements:

> • **2011 ICMA GMRA and Annex I elections.** The 2011 form is Voss Bank\'s standard master agreement for repurchase transactions. Voss Bank does not, as a matter of policy, negotiate under the 1995 ICMA GMRA or the 2000 TBMA/ISMA GMRA. If a counterparty proposes either legacy form, the desk should insist on migrating to the 2011 form. If the counterparty refuses, escalate to Legal.

> • **Bilateral and tri-party repo and reverse repo.** The playbook covers both bilateral structures (where collateral moves directly between the parties\' custodians or settlement accounts) and tri-party structures (including where BNY Meliora Trust Company, N.A. is appointed as tri-party custodian). The default structure under this playbook is bilateral; tri-party is elected only where specifically agreed and documented via a separate tri-party annexe.

> • **Buy/Sell Back transactions only where the Buy/Sell Back Annex is separately elected.** Buy/Sell Back treatment is not the default under this playbook. Where a counterparty specifically requests Buy/Sell Back treatment --- for example, to accommodate back-office systems that process Buy/Sell Back confirmations rather than classic repo confirmations --- the desk must refer the matter to Legal for negotiation of a separate Buy/Sell Back Annex. The desk should not agree to Buy/Sell Back treatment as part of the standard Annex I elections.

> • **Settlement through Clearstream Banking S.A.** (for Euro-denominated Eligible Collateral) **and The Depository Trust Company** (for USD-denominated Eligible Collateral). These are the standard settlement systems for the London Branch. Alternative settlement systems may be considered on a case-by-case basis, but any departure from these standard elections requires discussion with Operations (London) to confirm settlement capability.
**[1.3 --- How to Use This Playbook]{.underline}**
Each section below addresses a material commercial or legal term that arises in a typical GMRA negotiation. For each term, the playbook identifies three tiers of positioning:

> • **Preferred Position** --- the opening term Voss Bank will propose in a Turn 1 draft. This is the position that appears in Voss Bank\'s standard-form Annex I or in the initial mark-up of the counterparty\'s draft (where the counterparty circulates the first draft). The preferred position represents Voss Bank\'s optimal commercial and risk outcome. It is the starting point for all negotiations, and the desk should not concede the preferred position without first testing the counterparty\'s willingness to accept it.

> • **Fallback / Acceptable Range** --- the range of compromise the desk and Legal may agree without escalation to the Credit Committee. Within this range, the desk lead (at Director level) has full authority to agree terms on behalf of Voss Bank. The acceptable range is calibrated to reflect credit, regulatory, and market considerations, and to allow the desk sufficient flexibility to reach commercial agreement with a reasonable counterparty. Where the acceptable range is expressed as a numeric band (e.g., \$10,000,000 to \$25,000,000), any figure within the band --- including the endpoints --- may be agreed without escalation.

> • **Walk-Away Threshold** --- the point beyond which the term is unacceptable. Any counterparty proposal at or beyond this threshold requires escalation to the Credit Committee under Section 12 of this playbook. In certain cases, the walk-away threshold is absolute --- meaning that the Credit Committee itself is not authorised to approve a term beyond that point, and Voss Bank must either negotiate the counterparty away from its position or decline the transaction. In other cases, the walk-away threshold triggers a mandatory escalation, but the Credit Committee retains discretion to approve the term under exceptional circumstances.

The playbook also includes practical illustrations drawn from current or recent negotiations, particularly the ongoing negotiation with Meridian Capital Securities LLC (see Section 17 for a comprehensive counterparty-specific summary). These illustrations are intended to demonstrate how the playbook positions translate into real-world negotiation dynamics. They should not be treated as precedent for future negotiations with different counterparties, except to the extent that the underlying principles are of general application.
**[1.4 --- Current Active Negotiations]{.underline}**

This version of the playbook (Version 3.1) incorporates lessons from, and provides guidance specific to, the ongoing negotiation with **Meridian Capital Securities LLC** (CRD# 298417; EIN 83-2947561; LEI: 5493007XKBT49LP2QR12), a Delaware-organised SEC-registered broker-dealer. Meridian is a mid-tier US broker-dealer with a diversified secured funding business and an audited net capital of \$412,000,000 as at 31 December 2024.

The Meridian negotiation is at Turn 3 stage. Voss Bank circulated its Turn 1 draft on 14 March 2025. Meridian returned its Turn 2 redline on 28 March 2025, raising 23 individual mark-ups across the GMRA and Annex I. Of those 23 marks, 16 were non-commercial drafting changes and 7 were substantive commercial or legal proposals. Alistair Fenn of Calder Stone Partners LLP responded to 14 of the 23 marks by email on 4 April 2025, accepting 7 and providing Voss Bank\'s counter-position on the remaining 7. A call between Dana R. Castellano (Meridian\'s lead negotiator) and Henrik J. Lindqvist on 11 April 2025 resolved three of the outstanding commercial issues (sovereign haircut, corporate haircut, and margin threshold). Rachel S. Okonkwo of Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP (PAG) memorialised the call resolutions by email on 14 April 2025. Meridian\'s Turn 3 redline and updated issues list are due from PAG on 18 April 2025.

References to the Meridian negotiation are included as practical illustrations throughout this playbook. The counterparty-specific terms, issues tracker, and Annex I elections summary for Meridian are consolidated in Section 17.
**[Section 2 --- Base Currency, Transaction Types, and Netting]{.underline}**
**[2.1 --- Base Currency]{.underline}**

The Base Currency for all GMRA negotiations conducted by the London Branch is **USD**. This is both the preferred and the mandatory election. The desk does not have authority to agree a Base Currency other than USD without Credit Committee approval.

All haircut calculations, margin thresholds, exposure caps, cross-default thresholds, and any other monetary amounts specified in the GMRA or Annex I are denominated in USD unless otherwise stated. Where a Transaction involves non-USD Purchased Securities (e.g., Euro-denominated sovereign bonds), the relevant amounts are converted to USD at the applicable spot rate for the purposes of margin calculations, exposure monitoring, and threshold comparisons.

The selection of USD as the mandatory Base Currency reflects the London Branch\'s primary funding activities in USD-denominated repo markets and ensures consistency with the Branch\'s internal risk management systems, which are calibrated to USD exposures.
**[2.2 --- Buy/Sell Back Transactions]{.underline}**

The default election for Buy/Sell Back Transactions under the GMRA is **Not Applicable**. This means that the Buy/Sell Back Annex (ICMA form) is not incorporated into the GMRA as a default matter, and no Transaction entered into under the GMRA will be treated as a Buy/Sell Back Transaction unless the parties have separately agreed and executed a Buy/Sell Back Annex.

Where a counterparty requests Buy/Sell Back treatment --- for example, because the counterparty\'s back-office systems are configured to process Buy/Sell Back confirmations, or because the counterparty\'s internal legal framework treats Buy/Sell Back Transactions differently from classic repos for tax or accounting purposes --- the desk must escalate to Legal. Legal will assess whether the Buy/Sell Back Annex can be incorporated without adverse effects on Voss Bank\'s netting, HQLA, or capital treatment, and will negotiate any necessary amendments to the standard Buy/Sell Back Annex.

The desk should not agree to Buy/Sell Back treatment as a standard Annex I election. The structural differences between classic repo and Buy/Sell Back --- particularly with respect to the treatment of income payments and the mechanics of close-out --- warrant separate and careful consideration.
**[2.3 --- Agency Transactions]{.underline}**

The default election for Agency Transactions is **Not Applicable**. Voss Bank AG, London Branch, transacts solely as principal in all repo and reverse repo transactions. The London Branch does not act as agent for any other entity, and it does not accept counterparties acting in an agency capacity unless the underlying principal is separately identified, credit-approved, and documented.

If a counterparty proposes that it will act as agent for an undisclosed or disclosed principal, the desk must immediately escalate to Legal and the Credit Committee. Agency structures introduce additional credit, legal, and regulatory risks, including questions of counterparty identification for AML/KYC purposes, the applicability of close-out netting opinions, and the treatment of the agency relationship under SIPA (for US broker-dealers) or the FCA\'s client asset rules (for UK-authorised firms).
**[2.4 --- Netting]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred election is that **Paragraph 7(b) of the GMRA is elected**. Paragraph 7(b) provides for the netting of payment obligations arising under Transactions on the same settlement date and in the same currency. This netting mechanism reduces settlement risk by minimising the number and gross value of payment flows between the parties on any given day.

Netting applies on a **same-currency, same-settlement-date basis** only. The desk must resist any counterparty attempt to broaden the netting scope to include cross-currency netting (i.e., netting of payment obligations denominated in different currencies) or cross-settlement-date netting (i.e., netting of payment obligations falling due on different settlement dates). Cross-currency and cross-settlement-date netting introduce additional complexities, including FX conversion risk, timing mismatch risk, and potential inconsistencies with close-out netting opinions. Any proposal to broaden netting beyond the same-currency, same-settlement-date framework requires Credit Committee approval.

For the avoidance of doubt, the netting election under Paragraph 7(b) is distinct from the close-out netting provisions that apply upon an Event of Default or termination of the GMRA. Close-out netting is addressed in the body of the GMRA (Paragraph 10) and is not subject to election under Annex I. The enforceability of close-out netting is addressed in Section 15.1 of this playbook.
**[Section 3 --- Haircuts by Collateral Type]{.underline}**

Haircuts are among the most commercially significant terms in any GMRA negotiation. The haircut determines the relationship between the Market Value of the Purchased Securities and the Purchase Price, and thereby establishes the degree of overcollateralisation that protects Voss Bank (as Buyer) against a decline in the value of the collateral between margin call dates. Haircuts also have direct regulatory consequences: haircuts that are too low may cause received collateral to fall below the thresholds required for HQLA classification or may result in higher capital charges under the Basel III standardised approach for securities financing transactions.

The haircuts set out below apply to the initial calculation of Purchase Price. They are not intended to replace or limit the ongoing margin maintenance provisions of the GMRA (including the Margin Ratio, if separately agreed), but rather to establish the baseline overcollateralisation at the inception of each Transaction.
**[3.1 --- Sovereign Collateral]{.underline}**
**Parameter**                       **Position**
**Preferred Haircut**               **2.0%**
**Minimum Acceptable**              **1.5%**
**Walk-Away**                       Below 1.5%

**Eligible Sovereign Issuers.** Sovereign collateral is limited to obligations of G7 nations only --- that is, the United States of America, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, the Federal Republic of Germany, the French Republic, Japan, Canada, and the Italian Republic. Obligations of sub-sovereign issuers (e.g., US states or municipalities, German Länder, Canadian provinces) are not eligible as sovereign collateral for the purposes of this playbook, even where such obligations carry an explicit sovereign guarantee. Sub-sovereign obligations may be considered as a separate collateral category on a case-by-case basis, subject to Credit Committee approval.

**Minimum Credit Quality.** Eligible sovereign obligations must be rated **A--** (S&P Global Ratings) / **A3** (Moody\'s Investors Service) or better by at least one of those two agencies at the time of the relevant Transaction and continuously thereafter. If a sovereign issuer\'s credit rating falls below A-- / A3 during the term of a Transaction, the affected Purchased Securities cease to qualify as Eligible Collateral and must be substituted or the Transaction must be repriced. This requirement is implemented through the standard Eligible Collateral definition in Annex I, supplemented by Voss Bank\'s standard ratings-downgrade trigger clause.

**Haircut Application and Illustrative Calculations.** The haircut is applied as a discount to Market Value to determine the Purchase Price. Specifically, the Purchase Price is calculated as the Market Value of the Purchased Securities divided by one plus the applicable haircut percentage (expressed as a decimal). This methodology ensures that the haircut operates as a true overcollateralisation buffer --- the Seller delivers securities with a Market Value that exceeds the cash advanced by the Buyer by the haircut percentage.

At the preferred 2.0% haircut, illustrative sovereign collateral with a Market Value of \$100,000,000 produces a Purchase Price of **\$98,039,215.69** (\$100,000,000 ÷ 1.02). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,960,784.31, representing 2.0% of the Purchase Price.

At the minimum acceptable 1.5% haircut, the same collateral would produce a Purchase Price of **\$98,522,167.49** (\$100,000,000 ÷ 1.015). The overcollateralisation buffer narrows to \$1,477,832.51, representing 1.5% of the Purchase Price.

**Negotiation Dynamics.** For current negotiations (e.g., the Meridian negotiation), a midpoint of **1.75%** is within acceptable parameters and may be offered in a Turn 3 or later round as a commercial concession if the counterparty has proposed 1.5% and Voss Bank has opened at 2.0%. At the 1.75% midpoint, \$100,000,000 Market Value yields a Purchase Price of **\$98,280,098.28**, and the overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,719,901.72.

The desk should be aware that sovereign haircuts below 2.0% are increasingly common in the interdealer market for G7 sovereign collateral, particularly for US Treasury securities and German Bunds. The preferred 2.0% position may meet resistance from sophisticated counterparties, and the desk should be prepared to move to the midpoint range relatively early in the negotiation in exchange for concessions on other commercial terms (e.g., margin threshold, cross-default threshold, or repricing frequency).
**[3.2 --- Corporate Collateral]{.underline}**
**Parameter**                       **Position**
**Preferred Haircut**               **5.0%**
**Minimum Acceptable**              **4.0%**
**Walk-Away**                       Below 3.5%

**Eligible Corporate Bonds.** Eligible corporate collateral consists of corporate bonds rated **BBB+** (S&P Global Ratings) / **Baa1** (Moody\'s Investors Service) or better, with a residual maturity of **10 years or less** at the time of the relevant Transaction. Bonds with a residual maturity exceeding 10 years are excluded due to their higher duration risk and greater sensitivity to interest rate movements, which increases the probability of a material decline in Market Value between margin call dates.

Convertible bonds, contingent convertible bonds (CoCos), subordinated debt instruments, and any instrument with equity-linked features are excluded from the definition of Eligible Corporate Collateral regardless of credit rating or residual maturity. The desk should be vigilant for counterparty proposals that seek to broaden the definition of Eligible Corporate Collateral to include any such instruments.

**Haircut Application and Illustrative Calculations.** At the preferred 5.0% haircut, illustrative corporate collateral with a Market Value of \$50,000,000 produces a Purchase Price of **\$47,619,047.62** (\$50,000,000 ÷ 1.05). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$2,380,952.38.
At the minimum acceptable 4.0% haircut, the Purchase Price would be **\$48,076,923.08** (\$50,000,000 ÷ 1.04). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,923,076.92.

A counterparty counter of 3.5% sits at the extreme low end of Voss Bank\'s tolerance. The midpoint of 5.0% and 3.5% --- i.e., **4.25%** --- falls within the acceptable range and may be agreed without escalation. At 4.25%, \$50,000,000 Market Value yields a Purchase Price of **\$47,961,630.70**, and the overcollateralisation buffer is \$2,038,369.30.

**Walk-Away.** Haircuts below 3.5% are outside the acceptable range and constitute a walk-away unless the Credit Committee grants a specific counterparty exception pursuant to the escalation procedures set out in Section 12. The desk should note, however, that haircuts in the range of 3.5% to 4.0% fall within a \"grey zone\" --- they are technically within the walk-away boundary but below the minimum acceptable threshold. Any counterparty proposal in this grey zone must be escalated to the Credit Committee before agreement.
**[3.3 --- HQLA Eligibility Note]{.underline}**

The haircut levels set out in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 are calibrated to ensure that reverse repo collateral continues to qualify as Level 1 (sovereign) or Level 2A (eligible corporate) High-Quality Liquid Assets under the FINMA Liquidity Ordinance (LiqV) and the CRR delegated acts as applied via the Swiss \"equivalence\" framework. Maintenance of HQLA eligibility is critical to Voss Bank\'s compliance with the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirements imposed by FINMA.

The desk must not agree haircuts that would cause received collateral to fall below HQLA eligibility thresholds as periodically published by Treasury (Zürich). As of the date of this playbook, the current HQLA-floor haircuts are as follows:
> • **Level 1 sovereign collateral:** 0.5% minimum haircut.
> • **Level 2A corporate collateral:** 3.0% minimum haircut.

These floors represent the absolute regulatory minimum. The preferred and minimum acceptable haircuts stated in this playbook are intentionally set well above the HQLA floors to provide a margin of safety against regulatory reclassification. If a counterparty proposes haircuts that approach the HQLA floors --- even if the proposed haircut remains above the floor --- the desk must consult Treasury (Zürich) to confirm that the proposed level does not create adverse LCR or NSFR consequences.

Treasury (Zürich) updates the HQLA-floor haircuts at least semi-annually, or more frequently if there are material changes to the FINMA framework or to the CRR delegated acts. The desk should check the most recent Treasury circular before finalising haircut terms in any negotiation.
**[Section 4 --- Margin Thresholds]{.underline}**

The Margin Threshold determines the minimum aggregate Margin Deficit or Margin Excess that must exist before either party is obligated to make or entitled to receive a margin transfer. A well-calibrated Margin Threshold reduces the operational burden of frequent small margin calls while ensuring that material exposure imbalances are promptly addressed. The Margin Threshold is distinct from the haircut (which establishes the initial overcollateralisation) and from the Net Exposure Cap (which limits the aggregate credit exposure to a single counterparty).
**[4.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred Margin Threshold is **\$250,000 symmetric** --- that is, the same threshold applies to margin calls made by either party (Buyer or Seller), and no transfer of Margin Securities or Cash Margin is required unless the aggregate Margin Deficit or Margin Excess, as applicable, exceeds \$250,000. This threshold is applied on an aggregate, cross-Transaction basis (i.e., it is calculated with reference to the net margin position across all outstanding Transactions under the GMRA, not on a Transaction-by-Transaction basis).

The \$250,000 symmetric threshold is appropriate for the majority of Voss Bank\'s counterparties. It strikes a balance between operational efficiency (avoiding de minimis margin calls that consume settlement capacity without meaningfully reducing credit exposure) and risk management (ensuring that margin calls are triggered before exposure becomes material relative to the haircut buffer).
**[4.2 --- Acceptable Fallback --- Asymmetric Thresholds]{.underline}**

Where a counterparty (e.g., a regulated broker-dealer with net capital constraints, or a central bank with operational limitations on daily margin transfers) insists on a higher threshold for its own margin delivery obligations, Voss Bank may accept an **asymmetric** threshold structure. Under an asymmetric structure, the Margin Threshold for margin calls made by one party differs from the threshold for margin calls made by the other party.
Specifically, Voss Bank is prepared to accept the following asymmetric arrangement:

> • **Margin Threshold for Seller (counterparty) deliveries: up to \$500,000** --- acceptable provided that the **Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold remains at \$250,000**. Under this structure, the counterparty (as Seller) is not obligated to deliver Margin Securities or Cash Margin unless the aggregate Margin Deficit exceeds \$500,000, whereas Voss Bank (as Buyer) must return excess margin if the aggregate Margin Excess exceeds \$250,000.

> • This structure recognises that the counterparty bears a higher margining burden as Seller (because it is the party delivering margin in response to a margin deficit) while Voss Bank retains the benefit of a lower call threshold as Buyer (meaning that Voss Bank can call for margin at the \$250,000 level even though the counterparty cannot call for return of excess margin until the \$500,000 level is reached).

In the current Meridian negotiation, Meridian proposed \$500,000 symmetric at Turn 2. The acceptable resolution --- communicated to Meridian by Henrik J. Lindqvist on the 11 April 2025 call --- is to concede \$500,000 on Seller (Meridian) deliveries while holding the Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold at \$250,000. This outcome is within the desk\'s delegated authority and does not require Credit Committee approval.
**[4.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**
The following positions are at or beyond the walk-away threshold:

> • Any threshold above **\$500,000** for either party requires Credit Committee approval. The desk does not have authority to agree a Margin Threshold in excess of \$500,000 for either the Buyer or the Seller.

> • Any proposal to raise the Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold above \$250,000 is presumptively unacceptable absent exceptional credit quality of the counterparty (e.g., a sovereign wealth fund or central bank with a AAA credit rating). Raising the Buyer threshold above \$250,000 reduces Voss Bank\'s ability to call for margin promptly and increases the risk that a material margin deficit will accumulate before a call can be made.

> • Any proposal to eliminate the Margin Threshold entirely (i.e., to set the threshold at zero) should be viewed with caution, even though it is ostensibly more protective of Voss Bank\'s interests. A zero threshold creates significant operational burden and may result in a high volume of de minimis margin calls that strain settlement capacity. If a counterparty proposes a zero threshold, the desk should propose \$250,000 symmetric as a more practical alternative.
**[4.4 --- Margin Call Mechanics]{.underline}**
In addition to the Margin Threshold, the following margin call mechanics are standard Annex I elections and should be included in all GMRA negotiations:
> • **Margin call cut-off time: 10:00 a.m. London time.** This is the time by which a margin call must be received by the recipient party in order to trigger a same-day settlement obligation.

> • **Calls received before cut-off: same-day settlement.** If a valid margin call is received before 10:00 a.m. London time on a business day, the responding party must deliver the required Margin Securities or Cash Margin on the same business day.

> • **Calls received at or after cut-off: next business day settlement.** If a valid margin call is received at or after 10:00 a.m. London time, the responding party\'s obligation to deliver Margin Securities or Cash Margin is deferred to the next business day.

The 10:00 a.m. London time cut-off is non-negotiable. It aligns with the London Branch\'s operational cycle and with the settlement windows of the Branch\'s primary settlement systems (Clearstream and DTC). Counterparty proposals to move the cut-off to a later time (e.g., 12:00 noon London time or 10:00 a.m. New York time) should be resisted. If the counterparty insists on a later cut-off, consult Operations (London) to confirm whether a later cut-off can be operationally accommodated before making any concession.
**[Section 5 --- Net Exposure Cap]{.underline}**
**[5.1 --- Standard Cap]{.underline}**

The Net Exposure Cap is the maximum aggregate net credit exposure that Voss Bank is prepared to accept to a single counterparty under the GMRA. It is set on a counterparty-by-counterparty basis by the Credit Committee in Zürich, based on the counterparty\'s credit profile, the nature and expected volume of the trading relationship, and Voss Bank\'s overall portfolio concentration limits.

For the Meridian Capital Securities LLC relationship, the approved Net Exposure Cap is **\$1,500,000,000** (one billion five hundred million US dollars). This cap was approved by the Credit Committee on 7 March 2025 as part of the pre-negotiation credit approval for the Meridian GMRA.

The Net Exposure Cap is expressed as a single aggregate figure and is not broken down by Transaction type, collateral type, or tenor. It applies to the aggregate net mark-to-market exposure across all outstanding Transactions under the GMRA at any point in time, after giving effect to haircuts and any margin transfers.
**[5.2 --- Negotiation Guidance]{.underline}**

The Net Exposure Cap is not typically a negotiated term in the traditional sense. It is a unilateral credit limit set by Voss Bank to reflect its own credit risk appetite, and it is inserted into Annex I as a Buyer election. The counterparty is free to set its own exposure cap (if any) on its side, and Voss Bank will not object to a counterparty\'s unilateral cap unless it is so low as to render the trading relationship commercially unviable.
The desk should be aware of, and resist, the following counterparty proposals relating to the Net Exposure Cap:

> • **Bilateral cap.** Some counterparties will propose that the Net Exposure Cap be bilateral --- i.e., that it apply equally to both parties, so that neither party\'s aggregate net exposure may exceed the stated cap. This is inappropriate because the cap reflects Voss Bank\'s credit assessment of the counterparty, not a mutual assessment. A bilateral cap would constrain Voss Bank\'s ability to manage its own exposure unilaterally. The desk should reject bilateral cap proposals.

> • **Indexation.** Some counterparties (particularly US broker-dealers) will propose that the Net Exposure Cap be indexed to the counterparty\'s own net capital or regulatory capital ratios --- for example, that the cap be set at a fixed percentage of the counterparty\'s excess net capital under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Indexation introduces variability and unpredictability into the cap and creates a risk that the cap will decrease at precisely the time when the counterparty\'s credit quality is deteriorating (and when Voss Bank most needs the protection of a firm cap). The desk should reject indexation proposals.

> • **Periodic review.** The Credit Committee reviews Net Exposure Caps as part of its regular credit review cycle (typically annually, or more frequently if triggered by a credit event). The desk may agree to include language in Annex I stating that the cap is \"subject to periodic review,\" provided that such language does not create any obligation on Voss Bank to increase the cap or any right of the counterparty to request an increase.
**[Section 6 --- Substitution of Collateral]{.underline}**
**[6.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred position on substitution of Purchased Securities is that the Seller\'s right to substitute collateral requires **prior written consent** of the Buyer (Voss Bank). Consent may be given or withheld in Buyer\'s sole and absolute discretion, and no obligation to act reasonably or in good faith shall apply to Buyer\'s exercise of the consent right.

This position ensures that Voss Bank can assess the HQLA eligibility, haircut adequacy, and concentration limits of any proposed substitute collateral before the substitution takes effect. It also preserves Voss Bank\'s ability to refuse substitution at times of market stress, when the quality and liquidity of substitute collateral may be difficult to assess in real time.

The desk should propose the prior-consent position in all Turn 1 drafts. Counterparties with active collateral management programmes will frequently resist this position, arguing that the consent requirement impedes their ability to optimise their collateral pools. The desk should be prepared for pushback and should use the prior-consent position as a negotiating lever --- conceding it in exchange for concessions on other terms, such as haircuts or margin thresholds.
**[6.2 --- Acceptable Fallback]{.underline}**

    return ''.join(p.xpath('.//w:t/text()', namespaces=ns))

def paras():
    return root.xpath('.//w:p', namespaces=ns)

def find_para(predicate):
    for p in paras():
        t=ptext(p)
        if predicate(t): return p
    return None

def clone_rpr(p):
    for r in p.xpath('./w:r/w:rPr', namespaces=ns):
        return deepcopy(r)
    return None

def make_run(text, rpr=None, deleted=False):
    r=etree.Element(W+'r')
    if rpr is not None: r.append(deepcopy(rpr))
    t=etree.SubElement(r, W+('delText' if deleted else 't'))
    if text.startswith(' ') or text.endswith(' ') or '  ' in text:
        t.set('{http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace}space','preserve')
    t.text=text
    return r

def clear_content(p):
    for child in list(p):
        if child.tag != W+'pPr': p.remove(child)

def set_clean(p, text):
    rpr=clone_rpr(p)
    clear_content(p)
    p.append(make_run(text, rpr))

def replace_clean(predicate, old, new, label):
    p=find_para(predicate)
    if p is None: raise RuntimeError('Missing clean target '+label)
    text=ptext(p)
    if old not in text: raise RuntimeError(f'Missing text for {label}: {old!r} in {text!r}')
    set_clean(p, text.replace(old,new,1))

def replace_clean_full(predicate, new, label):
    p=find_para(predicate)
    if p is None: raise RuntimeError('Missing clean full target '+label)
    set_clean(p,new)

    global revision_id
    did=revision_id; revision_id += 1
    now='2025-04-17T12:00:00Z'
    de=etree.Element(W+'del', {W+'id':str(did),W+'author':author,W+'date':now})
    de.append(make_run(old,rpr,deleted=True))
    ins=etree.Element(W+'ins', {W+'id':str(did+1),W+'author':author,W+'date':now})
    ins.append(make_run(new,rpr,deleted=False))
    revision_id += 1
    return de,ins

def replace_tracked_full(predicate, new, label, comment_text=None):
    p=find_para(predicate)
    if p is None: raise RuntimeError('Missing tracked target '+label)
    old=ptext(p)
    rpr=clone_rpr(p)

111: **Paragraph 4(a) --- Margin Deficit / Margin Excess**
112: 
113: **4.1** The parties shall, on each Business Day (or at such other intervals as may be agreed), mark to market all outstanding Transactions by reference to the Market Value of the Purchased Securities and the Transaction Exposure in respect of each Transaction, each calculated in the Base Currency.
114: 
115: **4.2** If at any time the aggregate Cash Margin (if any) held by or on behalf of Buyer, together with the aggregate Market Value of all Purchased Securities held by Buyer (adjusted by the application of the relevant Haircut Percentage), is less than the aggregate Transaction Exposure of Buyer with respect to all Transactions then outstanding, a \"**Margin Deficit**\" shall be deemed to exist. The amount of such Margin Deficit shall be equal to the shortfall, calculated in the Base Currency.
116: 
117: **4.3** If at any time the aggregate Market Value of all Purchased Securities held by Buyer (adjusted by the application of the relevant Haircut Percentage), together with any Cash Margin held by or on behalf of Buyer, exceeds the aggregate Transaction Exposure of Buyer with respect to all Transactions then outstanding, a \"**Margin Excess**\" shall be deemed to exist. The amount of such Margin Excess shall be equal to the surplus, calculated in the Base Currency.
118: 
119: **Paragraph 4(b) --- Delivery Amount / Return Amount**
120: 
121: **4.4** Upon the existence of a Margin Deficit, Buyer may by notice to Seller (a \"**Margin Call**\") require Seller to transfer to Buyer Additional Purchased Securities or Cash Margin (or any combination thereof) in an amount sufficient to eliminate such Margin Deficit (the aggregate amount so required, the \"**Delivery Amount**\"). Notwithstanding the foregoing, no transfer shall be required if the Delivery Amount would be less than or equal to the applicable Margin Threshold specified in Annex II, Section 5(a) (being \$500,000 as of the date hereof).
122: 
123: **4.5 Upon the existence of a Margin Excess, Seller may by notice to Buyer (also a \"Margin Call\") require Buyer to transfer to Seller Equivalent Securities or Cash Margin (or any combination thereof) sufficient to eliminate such Margin Excess (the aggregate amount so required, the \"Return Amount\"). Notwithstanding the foregoing, no transfer shall be required if the Return Amount would be less than or equal to the applicable Margin Threshold specified in Annex II, Section 5(b) (being \$250,000 as of the date hereof).**
124: 
125: **4.6** Any Additional Purchased Securities transferred by Seller to Buyer pursuant to a Margin Call must constitute Eligible Collateral, and the Market Value of such Additional Purchased Securities (after application of the relevant Haircut Percentage) shall be at least equal to the Delivery Amount.
126: 
127: **Paragraph 4(c) --- Margin Call Timing**
128: 
129: **4.7** A Margin Call must be received by the other party by the margin call cut-off time specified in Annex II, Section 7 (being 10:00 a.m. London time as of the date hereof) in order for the resulting transfer to be required on that same Business Day.
130: 
131: **4.8** If a Margin Call is received before the cut-off time on a Business Day, the party receiving the Margin Call shall make the required transfer on that same Business Day.
132: 
133: **4.9** If a Margin Call is received at or after the cut-off time on a Business Day, or on a day that is not a Business Day, the party receiving the Margin Call shall make the required transfer on the next following Business Day.
134: 
135: **4.10** For the purposes of this Paragraph 4(c), a Margin Call shall be deemed to have been \"received\" when it is actually received by the recipient at the address, facsimile number, or electronic mail address specified in Annex II, Section 14 for the giving of notices. Each party shall use commercially reasonable efforts to acknowledge receipt of a Margin Call promptly upon receipt.
136:
